Basal Cell Skin Cancer
Basal Cell Skin Cancer (Basal Cell Carcinoma) is the most common type of skin cancer, characterized by abnormal growth of basal cells in the epidermis. It rarely metastasizes and is often treatable when detected early.<SEP>Basal cell skin cancer is a type of skin cancer that can recur or metastasize, requiring specific treatment strategies based on risk factors and recurrence patterns.

Skin Cancer
Skin Cancer is a broad category of cancers originating in the skin, with basal cell skin cancer being the most common subtype. It includes various types such as squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma.<SEP>Skin cancer is a broad category of cancers that originate in the skin, encompassing various types such as basal cell carcinoma, melanoma, and squamous cell skin cancer.<SEP>Skin cancer is a broad category of malignancies affecting the skin, including basal cell nevus syndrome and xeroderma pigmentosum-related conditions.

NCCN Guidelines for Patients
The **NCCN Guidelines for Patients** are a comprehensive set of **educational resources** provided by the **National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN)** through its website, **NCCN.org**. These guidelines serve as patient-focused tools designed to empower individuals and their caregivers with clear, evidence-based information about cancer care, treatment options, and management strategies. They are written in plain language to ensure accessibility and are grounded in the latest research and clinical practices from leading cancer centers.  

The guidelines cover a wide range of cancers and related conditions, including **breast cancer**, **chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)**, **cervical cancer**, **primary CNS lymphoma**, **gliomas**, and **throat cancer**, among others. They provide detailed explanations of treatment planning, testing procedures, and management protocols, such as **chemotherapy side effect management** (e.g., nausea and vomiting), **distress management during treatment**, and **fertility preservation strategies** (e.g., sperm banking and egg freezing) for adolescent and young adult patients.  

Additionally, the **NCCN Guidelines for Patients** include **patient advocacy guidance**, **care recommendations**, and **expert-recommended protocols** for conditions like **chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)**, **acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)**, and **basal cell skin cancer**. They also address specific therapeutic areas, such as **immunotherapy side effects**, **diagnosis and management of CLL**, and **management of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)**.  

These resources are intended to guide **cancer care decisions** for both patients and providers, offering trusted, actionable insights based on **evidence-based practices**. By integrating clinical expertise with patient-centered information, the **NCCN Guidelines for Patients** aim to improve treatment outcomes and support informed decision-making across diverse cancer care scenarios.

The Epidermis is the top layer of the skin, composed of basal cells and other cells, serving as a waterproof barrier and producing melanin for skin color.

Dermis

Hypodermis
The Hypodermis is the deepest layer of the skin, composed of fat and connective tissue, providing insulation and cushioning for underlying structures.

Squamous Cells
Squamous Cells are flat cells in the upper part of the epidermis, which are replaced by basal cells and contribute to the skin’s surface layer.

Melanocytes
Melanocytes are cells in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin, which determines skin, hair, and eye color and protects against UV radiation.

Adrenal Glands
Adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped glands located on top of the kidneys, responsible for producing hormones that regulate metabolism, stress response, and other critical bodily functions.

NCCN
The **National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN)** is a global nonprofit organization dedicated to advancing cancer care by providing evidence-based clinical guidelines, patient resources, and educational materials. Established as a leading authority in oncology, NCCN develops comprehensive standards for cancer prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and management across a wide range of cancers, including but not limited to kidney cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, breast cancer, lung cancer (Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer [NSCLC] and Small Cell Lung Cancer [SCLC]), head and neck cancers, colorectal cancer, cervical cancer, anal cancer, and Hodgkin lymphoma.  

NCCN’s guidelines address critical aspects of patient care, such as fertility preservation protocols, distress screening, test result access, and support services, while also incorporating recommendations for imaging standards, treatment planning, and genetic testing. The organization emphasizes patient education through tools like the **NCCN Guidelines for Patients**, a mobile app (NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer), and resources tailored to specific cancers, including protocols for immunotherapy side effects, prostate cancer management, and CLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia) care.  

Additionally, NCCN provides guidance on specialized areas such as bone cancer treatment, adrenal tumor management, and chronic conditions like chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). It also supports clinical research and trial information, ensuring patients and healthcare providers have access to up-to-date, actionable recommendations. By integrating clinical expertise with patient-centered resources, NCCN plays a pivotal role in standardizing cancer care and improving outcomes globally.

Pheochromocytoma
Pheochromocytoma is a tumor of the adrenal medulla that can be benign or malignant and is characterized by symptoms like high blood pressure and sweating.

Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1)

Imaging Tests
Imaging Tests are a category of diagnostic procedures that utilize radiological techniques, such as computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), ultrasound, and bone scans, to visualize internal body structures and detect cancerous abnormalities. These tests are critical for assessing the spread of cancers such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML), prostate cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, colon cancer, and leukemia beyond bone marrow, as well as monitoring treatment response and recurrence. They aid in staging cancers by evaluating organ involvement, including the brain, heart, liver, spleen, skin, and gastrointestinal tract, while minimizing radiation exposure where possible. Imaging Tests encompass specific applications, such as mammography and ultrasounds for breast tissue evaluation, CT and MRI scans for visualizing tumor extent and metastasis, and PET/CT scans for assessing disease progression. They are also used to detect complications like infections, bleeding, or organ dysfunction in conditions such as leukemia and regional squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). By providing detailed anatomical and functional insights, Imaging Tests guide treatment planning and improve patient outcomes across diverse oncological contexts.

CT Scan
**CT Scan (Computed Tomography Scan)** is a diagnostic imaging technique that utilizes X-rays and computer technology to generate detailed cross-sectional images of the body. This method combines multiple X-ray images taken from different angles to produce comprehensive views of internal structures, often enhanced with contrast material to improve visibility of tissues, organs, and abnormalities. CT scans are widely used to detect tumors, assess cancer spread, and evaluate conditions such as prostate cancer, ovarian cancer, colon cancer, and lymphoma. They are particularly valuable for identifying metastasis to abdominal or chest regions, enlarged lymph nodes, and the extent of disease in cancers like colon or ovarian cancer. CT scans are frequently employed as an alternative to MRI in specific scenarios, such as diagnosing CNS lymphoma when MRI is unavailable or not recommended. Additionally, they are often combined with PET scans for comprehensive cancer staging, offering insights into tumor size, location, and treatment response. The procedure is noted for its ability to provide anatomical details comparable to MRI, though it may differ in procedure duration and application specifics. Overall, CT scans remain a critical tool in medical diagnostics for visualizing internal structures, monitoring disease progression, and guiding treatment planning.

Radiation Therapy
Radiation Therapy is a non-invasive treatment modality that employs high-energy radiation (such as x-rays, photons, electrons, or protons) to target and destroy cancer cells, shrink tumors, and manage cancer-related symptoms. It is widely used across various cancer types, including prostate, cervical, anal, thyroid, non-small cell lung (NSCLC), brain (e.g., gliomas, CNS lymphoma), bladder, skin, and central nervous system cancers. The treatment is often administered over several weeks by a radiation oncologist and may involve advanced techniques like intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) to minimize damage to healthy tissue.  

Radiation Therapy is frequently combined with chemotherapy in chemoradiation protocols to enhance efficacy, particularly for localized or metastatic cancers such as anal, bladder, and cervical cancer. It may also be used alongside surgery or systemic therapies for advanced cases, such as squamous cell skin cancer, to eliminate residual cancer cells. However, it is associated with potential side effects, including fertility complications (e.g., ovarian damage), menopause, vision problems, cataracts, nervous system damage, vaginal stenosis, and localized tissue effects. For certain cancers, such as prostate or cervical cancer, it serves as a primary treatment to delay or avoid more aggressive interventions.  

The treatment’s application varies by cancer type: for example, external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) is used for prostate and cervical cancer, while whole-brain radiation therapy (WBRT) targets CNS lymphoma. In cases where surgery is not feasible (e.g., advanced thyroid cancer), Radiation Therapy provides a critical alternative. Its effectiveness is often balanced with strategies to manage side effects, ensuring optimal patient outcomes while minimizing harm to healthy tissues. Overall, Radiation Therapy remains a cornerstone of oncology, adapting to diverse clinical scenarios through specialized techniques and multimodal approaches.

Chemotherapy
**Chemotherapy** is a systemic treatment category that employs drugs to kill fast-growing cancer cells, often administered intravenously, orally, or intravesically, and is used across a wide range of cancers. It is a standard of care for conditions such as acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where it targets rapidly dividing cells, including both cancerous and normal cells. Chemotherapy is frequently combined with other therapies, such as radiation, immunotherapy, or surgery, to enhance efficacy. For example, it is used in conjunction with radiation for cervical, anal, and perianal cancers, and with immunotherapy for cancers with high tumor mutational burden or specific genetic markers.  

The treatment is commonly employed for cancers like bladder cancer, squamous cell skin cancer, inflammatory breast cancer, gliomas, ovarian cancer, and CNS lymphoma. In ovarian cancer, platinum-based drugs (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin) and taxanes (e.g., paclitaxel) are often used, either before or after surgery to shrink tumors or manage disease progression. For bladder cancer, chemotherapy may be administered systemically or intravesically, depending on the stage and type. In colon cancer, it is recommended for specific stages to reduce recurrence risk, while in CNS lymphoma, it is used alongside other therapies to target malignant cells.  

Common side effects include nausea, hair loss, and kidney damage, particularly with platinum-based regimens. Chemotherapy is also utilized for thyroid cancers, though its effectiveness is limited against most types, with radiation therapy often combined for aggressive subtypes like anaplastic thyroid cancer. The treatment typically involves cyclical administration to allow the body to recover between sessions, ensuring manageable toxicity while maximizing therapeutic outcomes. Overall, chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of oncology, tailored to individual patient needs and cancer characteristics.

Targeted Therapy
**Targeted Therapy** is a treatment approach that specifically attacks cancer cells while minimizing damage to healthy cells, often used in conjunction with chemotherapy. It is a category of systemic therapy that focuses on specific molecular targets on cancer cells, such as genetic mutations, proteins, or biomarkers like the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), to inhibit cancer growth and survival. This treatment method leverages drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells, often with fewer side effects compared to traditional therapies.  

Targeted Therapy is particularly effective for certain cancers, including thyroid cancers with specific genetic mutations or biomarkers, especially in recurrent or advanced cases resistant to radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy or other treatments. It is also an advanced option for thyroid cancers that have metastasized or do not respond to conventional therapies. Additionally, it is used in specific cases of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and other malignancies where molecular changes, such as FGFR3 mutations, are present.  

Examples of targeted therapy drugs include Balversa (erdafitinib) and Padcev (enfortumab vedotin-ejfv), which are designed to attack cancer cells with specific genetic alterations. This treatment is often recommended for patients ineligible for immunotherapy or clinical trials and is frequently combined with other therapies to enhance outcomes. By focusing on molecular features unique to cancer cells, targeted therapy aims to improve efficacy while reducing harm to normal tissues.

Immunotherapy
**Immunotherapy** is a systemic treatment approach that enhances the body's immune system to recognize, attack, and destroy cancer cells. It leverages immune checkpoint inhibitors, such as **Keytruda (pembrolizumab)**, **Opdivo (nivolumab)**, **Bavencio (avelumab)**, **Tecentriq (atezolizumab)**, and **cemiplimab-rwlc (Libtayo)**, to reactivate immune responses by blocking checkpoints like PD-1 and CTLA-4. This modality is particularly effective for cancers with specific genetic or molecular characteristics, such as **dMMR/MSI-H tumors**, **PD-L1–positive cancers**, and **TMB-H (high tumor mutational burden)** cancers.  

Immunotherapy is also used in combination with other therapies, including targeted treatments, for recurrent or advanced cases of **thyroid cancer**, **AML (acute myeloid leukemia)**, and **squamous cell skin cancer**. Key drugs like **rituximab** are employed to target specific proteins on cancer cells, making it effective for systemic treatment of **Primary CNS Lymphoma** and **HIV-related CNS lymphoma**. Additionally, it plays a role in **bladder cancer** management and is a critical component of systemic therapy for **bladder cancer**.  

The treatment is guided by biomarker profiles for specific cancer types, ensuring personalized approaches. For example, **checkpoint inhibitors** like **Keytruda** and **Opdivo** are utilized in advanced or inoperable **squamous cell skin cancer**, while **rituximab** remains a key drug for **primary CNS lymphoma**. Overall, immunotherapy represents a versatile and evolving category of cancer treatment, enhancing immune system efficacy to combat diverse malignancies.

PD-1 (programmed cell death protein 1) is a protein on immune cells that inhibits their activity, and its blockade by immunotherapies like pembrolizumab helps the immune system attack cancer cells.

Squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC) is a type of non-melanoma skin cancer that arises from squamous cells in the outer layer of the skin.<SEP>Squamous cell skin cancer (CSCC) is a type of skin cancer characterized by the uncontrolled growth of squamous cells, often treated with systemic therapies like chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy.

The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a U.S. federal agency that conducts and supports cancer research, including clinical trials and treatment guidelines.<SEP>The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a U.S. federal agency under the National Institutes of Health (NIH) that leads cancer research and provides information on cancer treatment and clinical trials.<SEP>The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a U.S. federal agency under the National Institutes of Health (NIH) that leads cancer research and provides information on cancer treatment, including anal cancer.<SEP>The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a U.S. federal agency under the National Institutes of Health (NIH) that leads cancer research, provides treatment guidelines, and offers resources on anal cancer.<SEP>The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a U.S. federal agency under the National Institutes of Health that conducts and supports cancer research, training, and education, including clinical trials and treatment guidelines.<SEP>The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a U.S. federal agency under the National Institutes of Health that conducts and supports cancer research, training, and education.<SEP>The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a U.S. government agency that funds and conducts cancer research, including clinical trials, to improve cancer treatment and prevention.<SEP>The National Cancer Institute (NCI) is a federal agency under the National Institutes of Health (NIH) that conducts and funds cancer research, provides treatment guidelines, and offers resources for clinical trials.

The U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM) is a federal agency that collects, provides access to, and advances biomedical information through databases and resources, including clinical trial information.<SEP>The U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM) is a federal agency that collects, provides access to, and advances biomedical information through databases and resources.<SEP>The U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM) is a federal agency that provides access to biomedical information and resources, including the ClinicalTrials.gov database.<SEP>The U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM) is a federal agency that provides access to biomedical information, including clinical trial databases like ClinicalTrials.gov.<SEP>The U.S. National Library of Medicine (NLM) is a federal agency that provides access to biomedical information, including resources on anal cancer and related conditions.

Clinical Trials
Clinical Trials are structured medical research studies designed to evaluate new treatments, therapies, or interventions for various cancers, including breast cancer, anal cancer, bladder cancer, primary CNS lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), squamous cell skin cancer, and pancreatic cancer. These studies involve human participants to assess the safety, efficacy, and long-term benefits of experimental therapies, such as chemotherapy regimens, immunotherapy, targeted therapies, and combinations like chemoradiation. Biomarker testing is often used to determine patient eligibility, ensuring treatments are tailored to individual biological profiles. Clinical Trials span different phases (Phase 1 to Phase 4) and may offer patients access to innovative therapies, particularly for advanced or high-risk conditions. They play a critical role in advancing medical knowledge, contributing to FDA approval processes, and improving outcomes for patients with weakened immune systems or limited treatment options. By testing new drugs, interventions, and therapeutic approaches, Clinical Trials drive advancements in cancer care and experimental treatments for a wide range of malignancies.

Local Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Local cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma refers to squamous cell skin cancer that has not spread to nearby lymph nodes and is typically treated with surgery.

High-Risk Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
High-risk squamous cell skin cancer has an increased risk of local recurrence and may require more aggressive treatment approaches.

data.content:
Very High-Risk Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
Very high-risk squamous cell skin cancer has an increased risk of local recurrence and metastasis (spread), often requiring specialized treatment strategies.

Photodynamic Therapy
Photodynamic therapy is a treatment that uses light-sensitive drugs and laser light to destroy cancer cells, often used for actinic keratoses and superficial skin cancers.

Topical Therapy
Topical therapy involves applying medications directly to the skin to treat conditions like actinic keratoses, often in the form of creams or gels.

Perineural Invasion
Perineural invasion is a condition where cancer cells invade surrounding nerves, often associated with high-risk or very high-risk squamous cell skin cancer.

ClinicalTrials.gov
ClinicalTrials.gov is a database maintained by the U.S. National Library of Medicine that lists ongoing and completed clinical trials for various diseases, including cancer.<SEP>ClinicalTrials.gov is a database of clinical trials registered and managed by the U.S. National Library of Medicine, providing information on ongoing and completed studies.

low-risk
Low-risk CSCC refers to a classification of squamous cell skin cancer with minimal likelihood of spreading, typically treated with less aggressive interventions like curettage or standard excision.

high-risk
High-risk CSCC denotes a more aggressive form of squamous cell skin cancer with a higher probability of recurrence or metastasis, requiring advanced treatments like Mohs surgery or systemic therapies.

very high-risk
Very high-risk CSCC is a severe classification of squamous cell skin cancer, often associated with deep tumor invasion, lymphovascular invasion, or compromised immune systems, necessitating intensive treatment protocols.

shave excision
Shave excision is a method of removing skin lesions by slicing the tumor off the surface of the skin, typically used for early-stage, low-risk CSCC.

standard surgical excision
Standard surgical excision involves removing the tumor along with a margin of healthy tissue, commonly used for low-risk CSCC when deeper invasion is not suspected.

radiation therapy
Radiation therapy uses high-energy beams to kill cancer cells and is recommended when surgery is not feasible, particularly for high-risk or very high-risk CSCC.<SEP>Radiation therapy uses high-energy rays to kill cancer cells, often employed for localized or advanced-stage prostate cancer.

platinum-based chemotherapy
Platinum-based chemotherapy is a systemic treatment involving platinum compounds to target cancer cells, often used in combination with radiation for advanced CSCC cases.

immunotherapy with an immune checkpoint inhibitor
Immunotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors enhances the body's immune response to cancer, preferred for certain high-risk CSCC cases where other treatments are insufficient.

lymphovascular invasion
Lymphovascular invasion refers to the presence of cancer cells in lymph or blood vessels outside the main tumor, indicating a higher risk of metastasis and influencing treatment decisions.

smoking
Smoking and vaping are risk factors for various cancers and can negatively impact cancer treatment outcomes.<SEP>Smoking is a significant risk factor for CSCC, increasing the likelihood of cancer development and complicating treatment outcomes due to its impact on healing and immune function.

The World Health Organization (WHO) is a global health organization that provides information and guidance on various health conditions, including kidney cancer and cancer treatments.<SEP>The World Health Organization (WHO) is a global health organization that provides information and guidance on various health conditions, including kidney cancer.<SEP>The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health, including guidelines and initiatives for cancer treatment and prevention.<SEP>The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health, including the classification of lymphomas like follicular lymphoma (FL).<SEP>The World Health Organization (WHO) is an international organization that classifies and standardizes medical conditions, including follicular lymphoma grades.<SEP>The World Health Organization is an international public health organization that provides guidelines and information on cancer treatment and management.

The American Cancer Society is a nonprofit organization that offers resources and information on cancer treatment options and patient support.<SEP>The American Cancer Society is a nonprofit organization that provides resources and support for cancer patients, including information on anal cancer treatment and research.<SEP>The American Cancer Society is a nonprofit organization that provides resources, support, and advocacy for cancer patients, including information on anal cancer treatment and research.<SEP>The American Cancer Society is a prominent organization providing resources and support for cancer patients, including information on treatment options and survivorship.<SEP>The American Cancer Society is a prominent organization providing resources and support for cancer patients, including information on treatment options, survivorship, and advocacy for anal cancer patients.

Local CSCC
Local CSCC refers to squamous cell skin cancer that has not spread to nearby lymph nodes and is typically treated with surgical or radiation methods.

Regional CSCC
Regional CSCC is squamous cell skin cancer that has spread to nearby lymph nodes, requiring more aggressive treatment options like surgery or systemic therapy.

Metastatic CSCC
Metastatic CSC, or squamous cell skin cancer that has spread to distant parts of the body, often necessitating systemic therapy or immunotherapy.<SEP>Metastatic CSCC is squamous cell skin cancer that has spread to distant parts of the body, often necessitating systemic therapy or immunotherapy.

Low-risk CSCC
Low-risk CSCC is a classification of squamous cell skin cancer with minimal likelihood of recurrence, often treated with less invasive procedures.

High-risk CSCC
High-risk CSCC is a classification of squamous cell skin cancer with a higher chance of recurrence or progression, requiring more intensive treatment strategies.

Very High-risk CSCC
Very High-risk CSCC is a severe form of squamous cell skin cancer that requires immediate and aggressive treatment to prevent further spread.

Mohs Surgery
Mohs surgery is a specialized surgical technique used to remove skin cancer layer by layer, ensuring complete excision of malignant tissue.

Platinum-based Chemotherapy
Platinum-based chemotherapy is a systemic treatment option used in combination with radiation therapy for advanced or high-risk squamous cell skin cancer.

Fine-needle Aspiration
Fine-needle aspiration is a biopsy technique used to extract fluid or tissue samples from suspicious lymph nodes to assess for cancer spread.

Core Needle Biopsy
Core Needle Biopsy is a procedure to remove tissue samples from a suspicious area, often guided by imaging techniques like ultrasound or MRI.<SEP>Core needle biopsy is a diagnostic procedure that removes a small core of tissue from a suspicious lymph node to confirm the presence of cancer cells.

Metastatic Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
Metastatic squamous cell skin cancer refers to cancer that has spread through blood or lymph to form tumors in other parts of the body. This condition is less commonly studied and requires systemic therapy as a primary treatment option.

Regional Squamous Cell Skin Cancer
Regional squamous cell skin cancer is cancer that has spread to nearby lymph nodes. Surgery to remove the tumor and affected lymph nodes is the recommended treatment, followed by radiation or systemic therapy.

National Comprehensive Cancer Network
The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides a feedback survey for patients to evaluate cancer information and resources.<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides cancer information and offers a patient feedback survey to improve resources and understanding.<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides clinical guidelines and resources for cancer care, including the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, which are trusted by healthcare providers and patients.<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides guidelines and recommendations for cancer treatment, including follow-up care and monitoring protocols.<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides guidelines and recommendations for cancer treatment, including the recommendation for clinical trials in primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides guidelines and resources for cancer care, including information on diagnosing and treating Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides guidelines for patients and healthcare providers regarding cancer care, including information on Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and its subtypes.<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network is an alliance of leading cancer centers that develops evidence-based cancer care recommendations used globally.

Follow-Up Exams
Follow-up exams are regular medical assessments conducted by doctors to monitor for cancer recurrence or new skin cancers, especially for patients who have completed treatment.

Platinum-Based Chemotherapy
Platinum-based chemotherapy involves drugs like cisplatin and oxaliplatin, which are effective against certain cancers but can cause kidney damage and peripheral neuropathy as side effects.<SEP>Platinum-based chemotherapy involves drugs like cisplatin and oxaliplatin, which can cause kidney damage and nerve toxicity.<SEP>Platinum-based chemotherapy is a specific type of chemotherapy that includes drugs like cisplatin or carboplatin, preferred for use with radiation therapy in certain cancer treatments.<SEP>Platinum-based chemotherapy is a systemic treatment using platinum compounds to kill cancer cells, often used for metastatic cervical cancer.

Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor
Immune checkpoint inhibitors are a class of immunotherapy drugs that block proteins preventing the immune system from attacking cancer cells, recommended for eligible patients with metastatic squamous cell skin cancer.

Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT)
Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is a specialized radiation technique that delivers high-dose radiation to small, precise areas over a short period, used for treating distant tumors causing symptoms.

Surgery
Surgery is a medical procedure used to remove as much of the glioma as possible, often combined with other treatments like radiation therapy and chemotherapy.<SEP>Surgery is a primary treatment method for thyroid cancer, involving the removal of the thyroid gland, either partially (lobectomy) or entirely (total thyroidectomy), depending on the cancer's characteristics.<SEP>Surgery is a primary treatment modality for bladder cancer, including procedures like TURBT and radical cystectomy, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor.<SEP>Surgery is a procedure to remove cancerous tissue, including secondary cytoreductive surgery for recurrent ovarian cancer.<SEP>Surgery is a treatment method for early or locally advanced NSCLC, involving the removal of cancerous tissue.<SEP>Surgery is a treatment method involving the removal of tumors and nearby lymph nodes, often followed by radiation therapy or systemic therapy to address residual cancer cells.<SEP>Surgery is a treatment modality for localized cervical cancer recurrence, often combined with radiation or systemic therapy.<SEP>Surgery is a treatment modality for prostate cancer, often considered for higher-risk cases, with potential complications and side effects that influence treatment planning.<SEP>Surgery is a treatment option for cancer that can be removed based on its size and location, particularly for localized thyroid cancer.<SEP>Surgery is a treatment option for localized cervical cancer recurrence, often followed by radiation or systemic therapy.<SEP>Surgery is the most effective treatment for thyroid cancer, involving the removal of the thyroid gland or affected lobes, often followed by hormone therapy.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (CSCC)
Squamous Cell Carcinoma (CSCC) is a type of skin cancer that requires regular monitoring and specific follow-up exam schedules, particularly for patients with high or very high risk factors.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)
Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a type of blood cancer caused by a genetic abnormality involving the BCR::ABL1 gene and the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome.<SEP>Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a type of blood cancer caused by a genetic mutation involving chromosomes 9 and 22, resulting in the BCR::ABL1 gene and the Philadelphia chromosome.

Philadelphia Chromosome
The Philadelphia Chromosome is a shortened chromosome 22 resulting from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, leading to the formation of the BCR::ABL1 gene fusion.<SEP>The Philadelphia chromosome is a shortened chromosome 22 formed by a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, which is a defining genetic abnormality in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML).<SEP>The Philadelphia chromosome is an abnormal chromosome (chromosome 22) formed by a translocation between chromosome 9 and 22, leading to the BCR::ABL1 gene fusion and hallmark of CML.

BCR::ABL1 Gene
The BCR::ABL1 gene is a fused gene resulting from the translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, which is the primary genetic cause of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML).<SEP>The BCR::ABL1 gene is a fusion gene resulting from the Philadelphia chromosome translocation, which produces a protein causing uncontrolled blood cell growth and is central to CML pathogenesis.

Blood Cells
Blood cells are the components of blood, including red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets, which play critical roles in oxygen transport, immune function, and clotting.

Skin Exams
Skin exams are medical procedures recommended for patients with skin cancer or high-risk conditions to monitor for recurrence or progression of the disease.

CML
CML (Chronic Myeloid Leukemia) is a type of blood cancer characterized by the overproduction of myeloid progenitor cells and the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a genetic fusion of the BCR and ABL genes.<SEP>CML (Chronic Myeloid Leukemia) is a type of cancer caused by the BCR::ABL1 gene and the Philadelphia chromosome, leading to the overproduction of immature blood cells and uncontrolled growth.

NSCLC
NSCLC (Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer) is a type of lung cancer characterized by slow growth and is often linked to smoking and exposure to carcinogens.<SEP>NSCLC (Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer) is the most common type of lung cancer, originating from cells lining the airways of the lungs and characterized by uncontrolled growth of lung carcinoma cells.

Myeloid Progenitor Cells
Myeloid progenitor cells are precursor cells in the bone marrow that differentiate into non-lymphoid blood cells, and their overproduction is a key feature of CML.

Lymphoblasts
Lymphoblasts are immature lymphoid cells that, when overproduced, can contribute to blast phase CML, a more aggressive form of the disease.

Myeloblasts
Myeloblasts are immature myeloid cells that, when overproduced, are referred to as blasts and are associated with blast phase CML and the progression of the disease.<SEP>Myeloblasts are immature white blood cells that mature into granulocytes (such as neutrophils) and are central to the development of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).

Blast Phase CML
Blast phase CML (BP-CML) is an advanced stage of CML characterized by the proliferation of immature blasts (myeloid or lymphoid) and requires more aggressive treatment strategies.

Lung Cancer
Lung Cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the cells lining the airways of the lungs, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth leading to tumors.<SEP>Lung cancer is a broad category of cancers affecting the lungs, encompassing subtypes like NSCLC and SCLC, with causes including smoking, secondhand smoke, and carcinogens.<SEP>Lung cancer is a malignant tumor originating from lung cells, with NSCLC being the most common type, and includes subtypes such as small cell lung cancer and neuroendocrine tumors.<SEP>Lung cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the cells of the lungs, with subtypes including non-small cell and small cell lung cancer.

Neuroendocrine Tumors
Neuroendocrine tumors are a type of lung carcinoma that arises from neuroendocrine cells in the lungs, often associated with specific genetic and molecular markers.

Alveoli
Alveoli are tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs, and their structure is critical for lung function and the progression of lung diseases.

Bronchi
Bronchi are the large airways that branch off the trachea into the lungs, forming part of the respiratory system and serving as sites for lung cancer development.

Bronchioli
Bronchioli are small airways that branch from the bronchi, leading to the alveoli, and are involved in the pathophysiology of lung diseases like NSCLC.

Trachea
The trachea (windpipe) is the main airway that connects the throat to the lungs, and its function is critical for respiration and the spread of lung cancer cells.

Airways
Airways refer to the entire network of passages in the respiratory system, including the trachea, bronchi, bronchioli, and alveoli, and are central to lung cancer progression and diagnosis.

Carcinoma
Carcinoma is a type of cancer that originates from epithelial cells, including lung carcinomas like NSCLC and neuroendocrine tumors.

Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC)
NSCLC is a type of lung cancer characterized by its origin in specific lung cells, with subcategories like adenocarcinoma, large cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma.

Early and Locally Advanced NSCLC
Early and locally advanced NSCLC refers to cancer stages 1, 2, and 3, where the cancer has grown into lung tissue or spread to nearby lymph nodes but not distant organs.

Metastatic NSCLC
Metastatic NSCLC is stage 4 cancer, where the disease has spread to other organs or tissues beyond the lungs.

Chemoradiation
Chemoradiation is a combined treatment modality that integrates chemotherapy and radiation therapy to address various cancers, particularly those in advanced or locally advanced stages. It is widely utilized for nonmetastatic and metastatic anal cancers, where it serves as a primary treatment for non-metastatic cases or is employed after specific chemotherapy regimens for metastatic instances. The approach is also critical for locally advanced cervical cancer, where concurrent chemotherapy and external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) are used to target cancer cells effectively, often as an initial treatment or to enhance outcomes in advanced stages. Similarly, chemoradiation is a standard strategy for bladder cancer, aiming to improve treatment efficacy, shrink tumors, and destroy cancer cells. For rectal cancer, it is a treatment category typically reserved for locally advanced cases. Additionally, it is recommended for nonmetastatic perianal and anal canal cancers that are not suitable for local excision. While some descriptions emphasize its use in advanced stages like metastatic anal cancer or locally advanced cervical cancer, others highlight its role in nonmetastatic settings, underscoring its adaptability across different cancer types and disease stages. The concurrent administration of chemotherapy and radiation therapy remains central to its mechanism, aiming to maximize cancer cell destruction and improve patient outcomes.

Supportive Care
Supportive care addresses symptoms and improves quality of life for pancreatic cancer patients, including pain management and psychological support.<SEP>Supportive care addresses symptoms and improves quality of life for patients with NSCLC, including managing side effects and enhancing daily living.<SEP>Supportive care focuses on relieving cancer symptoms and treatment side effects, improving quality of life without directly targeting cancer cells.<SEP>Supportive care focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life for cancer patients, addressing side effects of treatment and managing distress.<SEP>Supportive care involves managing symptoms and side effects of AML and its treatments to improve quality of life.<SEP>Supportive care refers to healthcare services designed to relieve symptoms caused by cancer or its treatments, aiming to improve the patient's quality of life through symptom management and emotional support.<SEP>Supportive care refers to the management of side effects and complications associated with cancer treatments, enhancing patient quality of life.<SEP>Supportive care refers to treatments aimed at relieving cancer symptoms and side effects, improving quality of life, and is often used alongside cancer therapies.

Lung nodules are small masses of tissue in the lungs that may be benign or malignant, requiring expert evaluation to determine if they are cancerous.

Lung Nodule
A lung nodule is a small mass of tissue in the lung, often detected through imaging, which may require further evaluation for cancer.

Lung Cancer Screening
Lung Cancer Screening is a medical procedure aimed at detecting lung cancer at an early stage, even before symptoms appear, through methods like low-dose CT scans.<SEP>Lung cancer screening is a medical procedure to detect lung cancer at an early stage, particularly for high-risk individuals.

Cancer-causing agents
Cancer-causing agents are substances or factors that increase the risk of developing lung cancer, such as radon, asbestos, and tobacco smoke.

Radon
Radon is a radioactive gas that can accumulate in buildings and is a significant risk factor for lung cancer.

Asbestos
Asbestos is a mineral fiber that, when inhaled, can lead to lung cancer and other respiratory diseases.

Arsenic
Arsenic is a toxic metal that, when exposed, increases the risk of developing lung cancer.

Beryllium
Beryllium is a lightweight metal that, when inhaled, can contribute to the development of lung cancer.

Cadmium
Cadmium is a heavy metal that, when inhaled or ingested, increases the risk of lung cancer.

Chromium
Chromium is a metal that, when exposed, can contribute to the development of lung cancer.

Nickel
Nickel is a metal that, when inhaled, increases the risk of developing lung cancer.

Coal smoke
Coal smoke is a byproduct of burning coal and contains harmful particles that increase lung cancer risk.

Soot
Soot is a fine particulate matter produced by combustion processes, which can contribute to lung cancer development.

Silica
Silica is a mineral that, when inhaled in fine particles, increases the risk of lung cancer.

Diesel fumes
Diesel fumes are emissions from diesel engines and contain harmful particulates that raise lung cancer risk.

Air pollution
Air pollution refers to the presence of harmful substances in the air, including fine particulates, which can increase lung cancer risk.

Fine particulates
Fine particulates are microscopic particles in the air that can penetrate deep into the lungs, increasing cancer risk.

Ozone
Ozone is a gas found in the atmosphere that, when inhaled, can contribute to lung cancer development.

Nitrogen oxides
Nitrogen oxides are pollutants that, when inhaled, increase the risk of lung cancer.

Sulfur dioxide
Sulfur dioxide is a gas emitted by industrial processes that can contribute to lung cancer risk.

Tobacco smoke
Tobacco smoke contains over 50 cancer-causing compounds and is the leading risk factor for lung cancer.

Secondhand smoke
Secondhand smoke is the smoke exhaled by others and the smoke from burning tobacco products, which increases lung cancer risk.

Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)
NSCLC is a broad category of lung cancer that accounts for the majority of cases, further divided into subtypes like adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC)
SCLC is an aggressive type of lung cancer that originates in neuroendocrine cells, characterized by rapid growth and early metastasis.

Adenocarcinoma
Adenocarcinoma is a malignant form of colon cancer that originates in the adenoma, characterized by the invasion of surrounding tissues and potential metastasis.<SEP>Adenocarcinoma is a subtype of NSCLC that arises from gland-forming cells in the airways, often associated with smoking and environmental factors.<SEP>Adenocarcinoma is a type of bladder cancer that originates in glandular cells, which are not typically found in the urinary tract but can develop in rare cases.<SEP>Adenocarcinoma is a type of cancer originating in glandular tissue, commonly associated with rectal polyps.<SEP>Adenocarcinoma is a type of cervical cancer originating in glandular cells of the endocervix, accounting for about 20% of cases.<SEP>Adenocarcinoma is a type of rectal cancer that develops from adenomas, characterized by gland-forming cells.<SEP>Adenocarcinoma is the most common type of colon cancer that originates from adenomas.

Squamous cell carcinoma
A type of cancer arising from squamous cells in the anal canal, commonly associated with HPV infection and a primary focus of anal cancer treatment.<SEP>Squamous cell carcinoma is a subtype of NSCLC that develops in the flat, scale-like cells lining the airways, commonly linked to tobacco use.

Large cell carcinoma
Large cell carcinoma is a subtype of NS,CLC characterized by large, undifferentiated cells that can appear in any part of the lungs.<SEP>Large cell carcinoma is a subtype of NSCLC characterized by large, undifferentiated cells that can appear in any part of the lungs.

Adenosquamous carcinoma
Adenosquamous carcinoma is a rare subtype of NSCLC combining features of adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma.

Sarcomatoid carcinoma
Sarcomatoid carcinoma is a rare and aggressive subtype of NSCLC with spindle-shaped cells resembling sarcomas.<SEP>Sarcomatoid carcinoma is a rare and aggressive subtype of NSCLC with spindle-shaped cells, often associated with poor prognosis.

SCLC
SCLC (Small Cell Lung Cancer) is a rapidly growing type of lung cancer strongly associated with smoking and exposure to carcinogens like radon and asbestos.

NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer App
NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer App is an organization offering digital cancer-related information and guidance through an application.<SEP>NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer App is an organization offering digital resources and information for cancer survivors and patients.<SEP>The NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app is a digital resource provided by NCCN to deliver patient-specific cancer information and guidelines.<SEP>The NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app is an organization offering mobile resources for cancer patients.

Carcinogens
Carcinogens are substances or agents that can cause cancer, such as radon and asbestos, and are linked to the development of lung cancer.

Secondhand Smoke
Secondhand smoke is the smoke exhaled by another person and the smoke from combustible tobacco products, which increases the risk of lung cancer.

Nicotine Addiction
Nicotine addiction is a condition that makes quitting smoking difficult and is associated with an increased risk of lung cancer.

Esophageal Cancer
Esophageal cancer can occur in the cardia of the stomach and is treated similarly to esophageal cancers.<SEP>Esophageal cancer refers to cancer originating in the esophagus, categorized into squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma, with progression stages from early to metastatic.<SEP>Esophageal cancer refers to cancer that originates in the esophagus, with two main types: squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. It is staged based on progression and metastasis.

Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a type of esophageal cancer arising from squamous cells in the upper and middle esophagus, often linked to chronic reflux.<SEP>Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a type of esophageal cancer that begins in the thin, flat squamous cells lining the upper and middle esophagus.

Esophageal Adenocarcinoma
Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is a type of esophageal cancer originating in mucus-producing cells of the lower esophagus, frequently associated with Barrett esophagus.<SEP>Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is a type of esophageal cancer that starts in the mucus-producing cells of the lower esophagus, often linked to Barrett esophagus.

Barrett Esophagus
Barrett esophagus (BE) is a condition where the normal squamous cells lining the lower esophagus are replaced by abnormal cells due to chronic acid reflux, increasing the risk of adenocarcinoma.<SEP>Barrett esophagus (BE) is a precancerous condition where the lower esophageal lining is replaced by abnormal cells due to chronic acid reflux, increasing adenocarcinoma risk.

Siewert Types
Siewert types are a classification system for tumors near the esophagogastric junction, used to determine staging and treatment approaches for esophageal cancers.<SEP>Siewert types are a classification system used in cancer staging to describe the location of tumors relative to the esophagogastric junction (EGJ) and stomach.

Stages of Esophageal Cancer
Stages of esophageal cancer categorize the disease based on tumor spread: early-stage (confined to the esophagus), locoregional (invaded wall layers or nearby lymph nodes), and metastatic (spread to distant organs like the liver or lungs).<SEP>Stages of esophageal cancer describe disease progression: early (confined to the esophagus), locoregional (spread to nearby tissues), and metastatic (distant spread to organs like the liver or lungs).

Esophagogastric Junction
The esophagogastric junction (EGJ) is the anatomical boundary between the esophagus and stomach, located beneath the diaphragm, critical for separating esophageal and gastric contents.

NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology
The NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology are evidence-based recommendations for cancer treatment, updated regularly to reflect new medical data.

NCCN Cancer Centers Index
The NCCN Cancer Centers Index lists member cancer centers affiliated with the National Comprehensive Cancer Network, providing information on specialized care.

Hodgkin lymphoma
Hodgkin lymphoma is a type of cancer characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells, affecting the lymphatic system.

lymphatic system
The lymphatic system is part of the immune system, responsible for fighting infections and diseases, and includes organs like lymph nodes, spleen, and bone marrow.

Classic Hodgkin lymphoma
Classic Hodgkin lymphoma is a subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells.

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma
Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma is a rare form of Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by popcorn-shaped cells, which can transform into other cancers.

Reed-Sternberg cells
Reed-Sternberg cells are large lymphocytes associated with Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, serving as a diagnostic marker.

popcorn-shaped cells
Popcorn-shaped cells are a characteristic feature of Nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, distinguishing it from other types.

Bile Duct Cancer Stages
Bile duct cancer stages refer to the progression of cancer within the bile duct, including measurements of tumor size and spread to nearby organs.

Guide T = Tumor
Guide T = Tumor is a document that outlines the staging criteria for bile duct cancer, including tumor size and spread.

Lymphoma Basics
Lymphoma Basics is a section explaining the fundamentals of lymphoma, including its classification and the role of the lymphatic system.

Follicular Lymphoma (FL)
Follicular Lymphoma (FL) is a slow-growing type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) that originates from B lymphocytes.

Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL)
Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) is a category of cancers that arise from lymphocytes, specifically B cells or T cells.

International Consensus Classification (ICC)
The International Consensus Classification (ICC) is an organization that groups lymphoma grades and provides treatment guidelines for follicular lymphoma.

Germinal Centers
Germinal centers are temporary structures in lymph nodes where B cells proliferate and undergo mutations, leading to the development of follicular lymphoma.

Centrocytes
Centrocytes are smaller B cells in the light zone of germinal centers, involved in the maturation process of lymphocytes.

Centroblasts
Centroblasts are larger B cells in the dark zone of germinal centers that divide rapidly and contribute to the formation of follicular lymphoma.

Lymphatic System
A network of organs and vessels that filters lymph fluid, plays a role in immune function, and facilitates cancer metastasis through lymph nodes.<SEP>The Lymphatic System is a major part of the body’s immune system, a network of tissues and organs that includes bone marrow, spleen, thymus, lymph nodes, and lymphatic vessels.<SEP>The lymphatic system includes lymph vessels and nodes that drain fluid from breast tissue and play a role in cancer metastasis.

Lymphocytes
Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell critical to the immune system, including B cells (which produce antibodies) and T cells (which fight infections and tumors).<SEP>Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell that plays a critical role in the immune system, including fighting infections and producing antibodies (B lymphocytes) or directly attacking pathogens (T lymphocytes).<SEP>Lymphocytes are white blood cells critical for immune function, including B cells (antibody producers), T cells (immune regulators), and natural killer cells (tumor/virus fighters).<SEP>Lymphocytes are white blood cells that help fight infection and disease, including B cells, T cells, and Natural Killer (NK) cells.<SEP>Lymphocytes are white blood cells that play a critical role in the immune system by producing antibodies and fighting infections, and they are the origin of lymphomas when they grow uncontrollably.

Bone Marrow
Bone Marrow is a component of the lymphatic system where lymphocytes originate and mature.<SEP>Bone marrow is a sponge-like tissue in bones that produces blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, through hematopoietic stem cells.<SEP>Bone marrow is a spongy tissue in bones where hematopoietic stem cells mature into blood cells, including lymphoblasts affected in ALL.<SEP>Bone marrow is the sponge-like tissue in bones where hematopoietic stem cells reside, responsible for producing all types of blood cells through a process called differentiation.<SEP>Bone marrow is the spongy tissue inside bones where blood cells are produced. It contains hematopoietic stem cells that differentiate into various blood cell types.

Spleen
Spleen is a component of the lymphatic system that filters blood and removes foreign material, including bacteria and cancer cells.<SEP>The spleen is an organ of the lymphatic system that filters blood, stores immune cells, and plays a role in immune responses and blood cell production.

Thymus
The thymus is an organ located in front of the windpipe where T-cell lymphoblasts mature, and its enlargement can cause breathing complications in T-ALL cases.<SEP>The thymus is an organ of the lymphatic system where T cells mature and undergo selection to ensure immune tolerance and functionality.<SEP>Thymus is a component of the lymphatic system that plays a role in the maturation of T cells.

Lymphatic Vessels
Lymphatic Vessels are components of the lymphatic system that transport lymph throughout the body.

B cells
B cells are a type of lymphocyte that produce antibodies to fight infections and are involved in the development of follicular lymphoma.<SEP>B cells are a type of lymphocyte that produce antibodies to neutralize pathogens like bacteria and viruses, and they are implicated in Cutaneous B-cell lymphoma (CBCL).

T cells
T cells are a type of lymphocyte that directly attack infected cells and play a role in immune responses.<SEP>T cells are a type of lymphocyte that directly kill infected or cancerous cells and regulate immune responses, and they are involved in Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL).

Natural Killer (NK) cells
Natural Killer (NK) cells are a type of lymphocyte that can recognize and destroy infected or cancerous cells without prior activation.

International Consensus Classification
The International Consensus Classification (ICC) is a collaborative system used by medical professionals to categorize lymphomas, grouping grades 1 and 2 as classic FL (cFL).

Follicular Lymphoma
Follicular lymphoma (FL) is a type of indolent (slow-growing) non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by abnormal B lymphocytes forming follicles in lymph nodes.

Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) is a broad category of cancers originating from lymphocytes, including follicular lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is an aggressive subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, which can be associated with transformed follicular lymphoma (FL) or FL grade 3B (FL3B).

Pediatric-Type FL
Pediatric-type FL (PTFL) is a variant of follicular lymphoma typically occurring in children, though it can also affect adults, with limited lymph node involvement and minimal symptoms.

Transformed FL
Transformed FL is a more aggressive form of follicular lymphoma that can progress into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), often requiring intensified treatment.

B Symptoms
B symptoms (fevers, night sweats, weight loss) are systemic symptoms of CLL that indicate disease activity and poor prognosis.<SEP>B symptoms refer to systemic symptoms like fever, night sweats, fatigue, and weight loss associated with lymphomas, including follicular lymphoma (FL).

Mouth Cancer
Mouth Cancer is a type of cancer that affects the lips, tongue, gums, and other parts of the mouth, classified under Head and Neck Cancers.<SEP>Mouth Cancer is a type of head and neck cancer that develops in the oral cavity, including the lips, cheeks, tongue, gums, and other mouth structures.<SEP>Mouth cancer is a type of cancer affecting the mouth area, with staging processes to determine prognosis and treatment options.

Head and Neck Cancer
Head and Neck Cancer refers to a group of cancers originating in the head or neck area, including the mouth, throat, and surrounding structures.<SEP>Head and neck cancer is a type of cancer that affects the jaw, teeth, gums, and other areas in the head and neck region, impacting treatment and dental care.<SEP>Head and neck cancer refers to cancers affecting the head, neck, and throat areas, including the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, and surrounding structures.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC) is the most common type of mouth cancer, originating from the thin, flat cells of the mucous membranes in the mouth.<SEP>Squamous Cell Carcinoma is the most common type of Mouth Cancer, arising from the squamous cells that line the mouth and throat.

Nasoph, a type of Head and Neck Cancer that originates in the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses.<SEP>Nasopharyngeal Cancer is a type of Head and Neck Cancer that originates in the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses.

Treatment Planning
The process of determining the most effective treatment options for a cancer patient based on diagnostic results and other factors.<SEP>The process of developing personalized treatment strategies based on diagnostic results, medical history, and genetic risk factors.<SEP>Treatment Planning is a category of medical strategy that involves selecting therapies based on test results, cancer type, and patient-specific factors.<SEP>Treatment Planning is the process of determining cancer management strategies based on test results, medical history, and patient-specific factors, including risks like fertility preservation and genetic testing.<SEP>Treatment Planning is the process of developing a personalized cancer care strategy based on test results, medical history, and other factors.<SEP>Treatment planning for CLL involves integrating diagnostic results, patient factors, and genetic profiling to select optimal therapies.

Biopsy
**Biopsy** is a diagnostic medical procedure involving the removal of tissue or fluid samples from suspected cancerous areas for laboratory analysis. This procedure is critical for confirming cancer diagnoses, determining tumor histology, and characterizing malignancies to guide treatment strategies. Biopsy methods include core needle biopsies, surgical biopsies, and other techniques tailored to specific organs or tissues, such as thyroid nodules, prostate tissue, breast tissue, ovarian tissue, brain tumors, bladder cancer, stomach lining, and metastatic sites. The extracted tissue or fluid is examined microscopically to identify cancerous cells, assess molecular features (e.g., DNA mutations, protein levels), and evaluate aggressiveness metrics like Gleason scores and Grade Groups. Biopsy also plays a role in diagnosing precancerous changes and providing data for personalized treatment planning. While generally effective, the procedure may carry risks such as infection, bleeding, or complications associated with invasive sampling. It remains a cornerstone in oncology for accurate diagnosis and therapeutic decision-making across diverse cancer types.

FDG-PET/CT
A hybrid imaging technique combining fluorodeoxyglucose (FD.M) PET and CT scans to identify cancer in lymph nodes and distant sites, requiring fasting before the procedure.<SEP>A hybrid imaging technique combining fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET and CT scans to identify cancer in lymph nodes and distant sites, requiring fasting before the procedure.<SEP>FDG-PET/CT combines PET and CT scans to provide comprehensive metabolic and anatomical information for cancer evaluation.<SEP>FDG-PET/CT combines PET and CT scans to provide detailed images of cancerous tissues and metabolic activity.<SEP>FDG-PET/CT combines PET and CT to detect cancer metabolism and spread.<SEP>FDG-PET/CT combines positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) to detect cancer metabolism and spread.<SEP>FDG-PET/CT combines positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) to provide detailed images of metabolic and anatomical structures, aiding in cancer detection and staging.<SEP>FDG-PET/CT combines positron emission tomography and computed tomography to visualize cancer metabolism, using a radiotracer called fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG).<SEP>FDG-PET/CT is a combined imaging test that uses radioactive tracers to identify areas of increased metabolic activity, aiding in the detection of extramedullary leukemia.<SEP>FDG-PET/CT is a combined imaging test using a radiotracer to detect cancer cells and assess their metabolic activity.<SEP>Imaging test to detect extramedullary leukemia, indicating AML spread beyond bone marrow.

Dental Exam includes imaging to assess oral health and detect early signs of mouth cancer.<SEP>Dental Exam includes x-rays or CT scans to assess oral health and detect early signs of mouth cancer.<SEP>Dental Exam is a procedure to assess oral health, particularly relevant for patients with head and neck cancers, as treatment can impact jaw, teeth, and gums.

Nutrition, Speech, and Swallowing Evaluation assesses functional impacts of cancer on daily activities.<SEP>Nutrition, Speech, and Swallowing Evaluation assesses how cancer affects a patient's ability to eat, speak, and swallow, guiding treatment planning.<SEP>Nutrition, speech, and swallowing evaluation assesses functional impairments caused by head and neck cancers, guiding dietary and rehabilitative care.

A diagnostic process to identify abnormal genetic changes (mutations) that may increase the risk of prostate cancer, including germline and molecular biomarker testing.<SEP>A process to identify harmful changes in genes, used to assess cancer risk and guide treatment, including hereditary gene testing and tumor testing.<SEP>Genetic Testing analyzes DNA to identify inherited genetic mutations that may increase cancer risk or affect treatment response.<SEP>Genetic Testing analyzes DNA to identify inherited mutations affecting cancer risk or treatment.<SEP>Genetic Testing identifies inherited cancer risks and mutations, aiding in personalized treatment planning for patients with a family history of head and neck cancers.<SEP>Genetic Testing is a category of diagnostic process used to identify hereditary cancer risks, particularly in cases of familial or genetic predisposition.<SEP>Genetic Testing is a diagnostic process analyzing DNA for mutations in genes like BRCA1, BRCA2, and Lynch Syndrome-related genes to assess hereditary cancer risks.<SEP>Genetic Testing is a diagnostic process that analyzes DNA to identify mutations in genes like BRCA1 and BRCA2, which are associated with hereditary cancer risks.<SEP>Genetic Testing is used to identify inherited genetic mutations that may increase the risk of developing bladder cancer, such as mutations in the TP53 gene.<SEP>Genetic testing involves analyzing DNA to identify inherited mutations that increase cancer risk.<SEP>Genetic testing involves analyzing leukemia cells for mutations, chromosomal abnormalities, and genetic changes to determine AML subtypes, prognosis, and targeted treatment options.<SEP>Genetic testing refers to the analysis of DNA to detect inherited mutations, such as BRCA mutations, which are critical for understanding hereditary cancer risks and treatment planning.<SEP>Tests to detect gene mutations or abnormal chromosomes that contribute to AML diagnosis and treatment planning.
