HPV Testing is a diagnostic category used to identify HPV infections, which are linked to specific cancer subtypes and influence treatment decisions.<SEP>HPV testing is a diagnostic procedure used to detect human papillomavirus (HPV) in tumor tissue, which is critical for staging and treatment planning in oropharyngeal cancers.

HPV-Related Cancer
HPV-Related Cancer is a specific cancer category linked to human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, characterized by distinct tumor features and improved treatment responses.

Panoramic dental x-ray
A panoramic dental x-ray captures a wide view of the entire mouth, including teeth, jaw structures, and surrounding tissues, commonly used for dental treatment planning.

Scoping procedures
Scoping procedures involve inserting a flexible tube with a camera into the body to visualize internal structures, often used for imaging the oropharynx and guiding biopsies.

Fiberoptic nasopharyngolaryngoscopy
This procedure uses a fiberoptic scope to examine the larynx and nearby structures, helping diagnose conditions like vocal cord abnormalities or cancerous growths.

Laryngoscopy
Laryngoscopy involves using a specialized scope to visualize the larynx and hypopharynx, enabling detection of tumors and assessment of vocal cord function.

Contrast material
Contrast material enhances imaging test accuracy by improving visibility of internal structures, though it may cause allergic reactions in some patients.<SEP>Contrast material is a substance used in imaging to enhance the visibility of internal organs and structures, aiding in the diagnosis of various conditions by improving image clarity.

Imaging
Imaging encompasses various diagnostic techniques such as MRI, CT, ultrasound, and PET scans, used to visualize internal body structures and detect abnormalities like tumors.<SEP>Imaging is a diagnostic procedure used to determine the extent of cervical cancer before treatment, involving techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound.<SEP>Imaging is a diagnostic test used to identify and monitor gliomas, providing visual information about tumor location and size.<SEP>Imaging refers to diagnostic procedures like CT, MRI, or PET/CT scans used to detect cancer recurrence or metastasis.<SEP>Imaging refers to diagnostic procedures like CT, MRI, or PET/CT scans used to detect cancer recurrence or spread.<SEP>Imaging refers to diagnostic techniques like CT, MRI, and ultrasound used to visualize internal body structures and detect cancerous growths.<SEP>Imaging refers to diagnostic tests like CT scans and MRIs used to monitor cancer progression, detect metastasis, and evaluate treatment effectiveness.<SEP>Imaging refers to medical techniques like X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs used to visualize internal structures and detect abnormalities such as cancer.<SEP>Imaging refers to techniques like CT, MRI, and ultrasound used to visualize internal body structures and detect cancerous growths.<SEP>Imaging refers to the use of medical scans like MRI or CT to create images of the brain and detect tumors or abnormalities.<SEP>Imaging techniques are used to determine the extent of cervical cancer and guide treatment decisions.<SEP>Imaging techniques like CT scans and MRIs are used for surveillance and staging metastatic anal cancer, recommended annually for 3 years post-treatment.<SEP>Imaging techniques such as X-rays, CT scans, or MRI are used to visualize the bladder and surrounding areas to assess the extent and spread of cancer.

Diagnostic test
Diagnostic tests are medical procedures used to identify diseases or conditions, including imaging studies and endoscopic exams, to assess the presence and extent of conditions like cancer.

Fiberoptic Laryngoscopy
A medical procedure using a flexible scope to examine the throat, typically performed with numbing medicine and taking less than 1 minute.

Direct Laryngoscopy
A detailed medical exam performed under general anesthesia to examine the throat and take biopsies, allowing deeper visualization of the larynx.

Esophagoscopy
A procedure to examine the esophagus for abnormal growths, performed under anesthesia to assess swallowing tube health.

Bronchoscopy
A diagnostic procedure to examine the airway, trachea, and bronchi, often used to detect cancer or perform treatments under anesthesia.

Panendoscopy
A comprehensive procedure combining laryngoscopy, pharyng, esophagoscopy, and bronchoscopy to thoroughly examine the head and neck region for tumors or abnormalities.<SEP>A comprehensive procedure combining laryngoscopy, pharyngoscopy, esophagoscopy, and bronchoscopy to thoroughly examine the head and neck region for tumors or abnormalities.

Tumor p16 (HPV) Testing
A diagnostic test to detect HPV-associated tumors in the throat, using p16 as a marker for human papillomavirus infection.

AJCC
AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) is an organization that developed the staging system for cancer, including TNM scores and prognostic staging frameworks.<SEP>AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) is an organization that developed the staging system for cancer, including TNM scores and prognostic staging.<SEP>The American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) is an organization that developed a standardized staging system for cancer, which helps determine treatment options and prognosis.

Cell-free DNA Testing
Cell-free DNA testing analyzes circulating tumor DNA in blood samples to monitor cancer progression, treatment response, and recurrence, though it is not yet a standard diagnostic tool.

Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Therapy
Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy is an advanced immunotherapy targeting proteins like PD-1 and PD-L1 to enhance the immune system's ability to fight cancer cells.<SEP>Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy is an advanced immunotherapy targeting proteins like PD-1 and PD-L3 to enhance the immune system's ability to fight cancer cells.

PDL1
PDL1 (Programmed Death-Ligand 1) is a protein expressed on cancer cells that interacts with immune checkpoints, making it a key biomarker for selecting patients for immunotherapy.

Prognosis
ProNone<SEP>Prognosis is a category that refers to the predicted course and outcome of a patient's cancer, influenced by staging, biomarker testing, and treatment approaches.<SEP>Prognosis is the predicted course and outcome of a disease, distinguishing it from diagnosis, and is influenced by factors like cancer stage, biomarkers, and treatment response.<SEP>Prognosis predicts the likely course and outcome of prostate cancer, guiding treatment decisions based on risk assessments and molecular biomarker results.<SEP>Prognosis refers to the likely course and outcome of a cancer, determined by factors like staging, biomarker testing, and the patient's overall health.

Staging
A process to determine the extent of cancer spread, crucial for tailoring treatment options for bladder and anal cancers.<SEP>Staging is a category used to describe the extent of cancer spread, combining factors like tumor size, lymph node involvement, and metastasis.<SEP>Staging is a classification system used to describe the extent of cancer spread within the bladder wall.<SEP>Staging is the process of determining cancer severity using the TNM system, guiding treatment plans and predicting outcomes.<SEP>Staging is the process of determining the extent of cancer (T, N, M, G) to guide treatment plans and predict patient outcomes, often using systems like the AJCC staging framework.<SEP>Staging is the process of determining the extent of cancer (tumor, node, metastasis) to guide treatment decisions and predict outcomes for anal cancer patients.<SEP>Staging is the process of determining the extent of cervical cancer based on imaging results, biopsies, and other diagnostic tests to guide treatment decisions.

Dental Cleanings and Checkups
Dental cleanings and checkups are preventive care measures recommended for patients with head and neck cancer to maintain oral health during treatment.

Online Portals
Online Portals is a category of digital tools enabling patients to access medical information, test results, and healthcare resources remotely.<SEP>Online portals provide patients with secure access to medical records, test results, and treatment information, enhancing communication between patients and healthcare providers.

Survey
Surveys are tools used to gather patient feedback on medical guidelines and care experiences, helping improve the quality and relevance of patient-centered resources.

Clinical Stage
Clinical stage refers to the rating given before any treatment, based on physical exams, biopsies, and imaging tests to determine the extent of cancer.

Pathologic Stage
Pathologic stage is determined after surgery by examining tissue removed during the procedure, providing more accurate details about cancer spread.

TNM System
A classification system used in cancer staging to describe tumor size, lymph node involvement, and metastasis, guiding treatment decisions.<SEP>The TN, N, and M scores are combined to assign the cancer one of the following stages: 0, I (1), II (2), III (3), or IV (4).<SEP>The TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system is a classification framework used to stage breast cancer based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and metastasis.<SEP>The TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system is a standardized framework for describing cancer progression, categorizing tumors based on size (T), lymph node involvement (N), and distant metastasis (M).<SEP>The TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system is a standardized framework used to describe the extent of cancer spread, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and distant metastasis.<SEP>The TNM System is a standardized categorization framework used in cancer staging, where T (tumor), N (nodes), and M (metastasis) scores define the stage and progression of cancer.<SEP>The TNM System is a standardized method used to stage cancer, assessing the extent of the tumor (T), involvement of lymph nodes (N), and presence of metastasis (M) to determine the cancer's stage.<SEP>The TNM system (tumor, node, metastasis) is a standardized framework used to stage throat cancer based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and metastasis.<SEP>The TNM system is a classification method used to stage bone cancers by evaluating the tumor (T), regional lymph nodes (N), and distant metastasis (M).<SEP>The TNM system is a standardized cancer staging framework that uses T (tumor size), N (lymph node involvement), and M (metastasis) to classify cancer stages.

p16-Positive
p16-positive cancer is HPV-related (HPV-mediated) and starts in the oropharynx, with distinct staging criteria compared to p16-negative cancers.

p16-Negative
p16-negative cancer is not caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) and uses the TNM staging system for squamous cell carcinoma without p16 testing.

Numbered Stages
Numbered stages (0-4) are based on TNM scores, indicating the progression of cancer from early (stage 0) to advanced (stage 4).

Locoregional
Locoregional disease refers to cancer that has spread to nearby tissues, organs, or lymph nodes in the head and neck region.

Head and Neck
Head and neck refers to the anatomical region containing lymph nodes, tumors, and structures like the carotid artery, where cancer often spreads.

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)
Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing blood cancer that originates in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, and affects bone marrow function.<SEP>Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing blood cancer that originates in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, and disrupts normal blood cell production by overproducing immature lymphoblasts.<SEP>Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a type of blood cancer that affects lymphocytes, leading to the overproduction of immature lymphoblasts.<SEP>Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a type of blood cancer that originates in lymphocytes, leading to the overproduction of immature lymphoblasts.<SEP>Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a fast-growing blood cancer characterized by the overproduction of immature lymphocytes (lymphoblasts) in the bone marrow, leading to impaired normal blood cell function.

B-cell ALL
B-cell ALL (Burkitt leukemia) is a rare subtype of ALL that originates from B-cell lymphoblasts, primarily affecting lymph nodes rather than bone marrow.<SEP>B-cell ALL is a subtype of ALL that arises from B-cell lymphocytes, characterized by the proliferation of B-cell lymphoblasts in the bone marrow and lymph nodes.<SEP>B-cell ALL is a subtype of ALL that originates from B-cell lymphocytes and is more common than T-cell ALL.<SEP>B-cell ALL is a subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukemia that originates in B lymphocytes, characterized by the overproduction of immature B-cell lymphoblasts.

T-cell ALL
T-cell ALL (T-ALL) is a subtype of ALL that arises from T-cell lymphoblasts, often involving the thymus and leading to enlarged thymus complications.<SEP>T-cell ALL is a subtype of ALL that originates from T-cell lymphocytes and can cause an enlarged thymus, leading to breathing difficulties.<SEP>T-cell ALL is a subtype of ALL that originates from T-cell lymphocytes, often causing an enlarged thymus and potential respiratory complications.<SEP>T-cell ALL is a subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukemia that originates in T lymphocytes, marked by the proliferation of immature T-cell lymphoblasts.

Pediatric
Pediatric refers to ALL cases in infants, children, and young adults under 18 years of age, as well as certain adolescents and young adults (AYAs).<SEP>Pediatric refers to ALL cases in infants, children, and young adults under 18 years of age, including certain adolescents and young adults (AYAs) in treatment.<SEP>Pediatric refers to ALL cases in infants, children, and young adults under 18 years old, with specialized treatment approaches compared to adult cases.

AYA
AYA (Adolescents and Young Adults) refers to individuals aged 15 to 39 years at the time of initial cancer diagnosis, who may be treated in either pediatric or adult centers.<SEP>AYA (Adolescents and Young Adults) refers to individuals aged 15 to 39 years diagnosed with ALL, who may receive treatment in either pediatric or adult care settings.

National Comprehensive Cancer Network® (NCCN®)
The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides guidelines and resources for cancer treatment, including information on acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides guidelines, educational resources, and support for cancer treatment, including information on acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).<SEP>The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) is an organization that provides guidelines, resources, and expertise for cancer treatment and patient care.

ALL
ALL (Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a fast-growing cancer that originates in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, characterized by the overproduction of immature lymphoblasts that crowd out normal blood cell production.<SEP>ALL (Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a type of cancer affecting lymphoid progenitor cells, leading to the overproduction of lymphocytes.

Rectal Cancer
Rectal Cancer is a type of cancer originating in the rectum, often treated with transabdominal surgery, chemotherapy, or chemoradiation.<SEP>Rectal cancer is a malignant tumor that originates in the rectum, often starting as a polyp like an adenoma.<SEP>Rectal cancer is a type of cancer originating in the rectum, often requiring staging procedures like MRI and CT scans to assess tumor depth, lymph node involvement, and metastasis to distant organs.<SEP>Rectal cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the rectum, part of the large intestine, and can be cured if detected early.

B-ALL
B-ALL (B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a subtype of ALL that originates in B-cell lymphocytes and is the most common type of ALL.<SEP>B-ALL (B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a subtype of ALL that originates in B-cell lymphocytes, more common than T-ALL.

T-ALL
T-ALL (T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a less common ALL subtype with treatment options including chemotherapy and clinical trials.<SEP>T-ALL (T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a subtype of ALL that originates in T-cell lymphocytes and is less common than B-ALL.<SEP>T-ALL (T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a subtype of ALL that originates in T-cell lymphocytes, less common than B-ALL.<SEP>T-None (T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia) is a subtype of ALL that originates in T-cell lymphocytes and is less common than B-ALL.

Testing for ALL
Testing for ALL involves diagnostic procedures to confirm the presence of the disease and determine treatment plans.<SEP>Testing for ALL provides an overview of diagnostic tests, fertility impacts, and genetic mutation testing for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL).

Infant ALL Treatment
Infant ALL treatment is a specialized approach for children under 12 months of age, differing from other age groups.

BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL Treatment
BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL treatment targets the BCR::ABL protein caused by the BCR::ABL1 gene, using systemic therapies.

BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL Treatment
BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL treatment focuses on managing these specific subtypes of B-ALL through clinical trials.

Hyperplastic Polyps
Hyperplastic polyps are non-cancerous growths in the colon and rectum that rarely develop into cancer.

Inflammatory Polyps
Inflammatory polyps are non-cancerous growths in the colon and rectum that rarely turn into cancer.

Mismatch Repair (MMR) Genes
Mismatch repair genes are responsible for correcting DNA damage; mutations in these genes are associated with Lynch syndrome and certain types of rectal cancer.

Microsatellite Instability-High (MSI-H)
MSI-H is a biomarker indicating defects in mismatch repair genes, which can influence treatment strategies for rectal cancer.<SEP>Microsatellite Instability-High (MSI-H) is a genetic feature that can be targeted with specific therapies for thyroid cancer.

Microsatellite Stable (MSS)
MSS refers to tumors with normal mismatch repair gene function, distinguishing them from MSI-H tumors.

Mismatch Repair Proficient (pMMR)
pMMR describes tumors with intact mismatch repair gene function, contrasting with MSI-H and dMMR tumors.

Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA)
CEA is a protein biomarker often elevated in colorectal cancer, used to monitor treatment response and disease progression.<SEP>CEA is a protein found in blood that may be elevated in colorectal cancer, used for monitoring treatment response and recurrence.

Circulating Tumor DNA (ctDNA)
ctDNA is DNA released by tumor cells into the bloodstream, used in liquid biopsy tests to detect residual cancer cells after treatment.<SEP>ctDNA is a biomarker derived from cancer cells in the bloodstream, used to detect and monitor cancer progression and treatment efficacy.<SEP>ctDNA is a biomarker derived from cancer cells in the bloodstream, used to detect and monitor cancer progression.

Liquid Biopsy
Liquid Biopsy is a non-invasive diagnostic method that analyzes blood samples to detect cancer cells, often used for monitoring metastasis in prostate cancer.<SEP>Liquid biopsy is a non-invasive diagnostic method analyzing circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in blood to assess cancer presence and treatment response.

CT
CT (Computed Tomography) is a diagnostic imaging method that uses radiation to detect cancer spread to organs like the liver, lungs, or other areas, typically involving contrast agents for clearer images.<SEP>CT (Computed Tomography) is a diagnostic imaging method using radiation to detect cancer metastasis to organs like the liver, lungs, or other areas, typically involving contrast agents for clearer images.<SEP>CT (Computed Tomography) is an imaging technique that uses x-rays to create detailed cross-sectional images of the body, often used as an alternative to MRI when necessary.

Endorectal Ultrasound
Endorectal ultrasound is a procedure using sound waves to assess rectal cancer extent in the pelvis, guiding biopsies of lymph nodes or surrounding tissues and aiding in local staging.<SEP>Endorectal ultrasound is a procedure using sound waves to evaluate rectal cancer extent, involving a probe inserted into the rectum to create images of pelvic structures and guide biopsies.

dMMR
dMMR (DNA Mismatch Repair Deficiency) is a biomarker indicating defective DNA repair mechanisms in cancer cells, associated with Lynch syndrome and specific rectal cancer subtypes responsive to targeted therapies.<SEP>dMMR (DNA Mismatch Repair Deficiency) is a biomarker indicating defective DNA repair mechanisms, linked to Lynch syndrome and specific rectal cancer subtypes requiring targeted therapies.

MSI-H
MSI-H (Microsatellite Instability-High) is a biomarker reflecting DNA repair defects in cancer cells, linked to Lynch syndrome and potential responsiveness to immunotherapy in rectal cancer.<SEP>MSI-H (Microsatellite Instability-High) is a biomarker reflecting DNA repair defects, associated with Lynch syndrome and potential responsiveness to immunotherapy in rectal cancer.

Premature Ovarian Insufficiency (POI)
Premature Ovarian Insufficiency is a condition where ovaries lose function before age 40, often caused by radiation therapy, leading to infertility and hormonal imbalances in female cancer patients.<SEP>Premature Ovarian Insufficiency is a condition where ovaries stop functioning normally before age 40, often caused by radiation therapy, leading to infertility and hormonal imbalances.

Radiation-Induced Premature Menopause
Radiation-Induced Premature Menopause is a side effect of rectal cancer radiation therapy, causing ovarian hormone production to cease and impacting fertility and reproductive health.

Sperm Banking
Sperm Banking is a fertility preservation method involving freezing and storing sperm for future use after cancer treatment.<SEP>Sperm Banking is a fertility preservation technique involving cryopreservation of semen for future reproductive use.<SEP>Sperm banking is a fertility preservation method involving semen cryopreservation (freezing) for later use, enabling future conception after cancer treatment.<SEP>Sperm banking is a fertility preservation method where semen is frozen using cryopreservation to enable future reproduction for cancer patients undergoing treatments that may affect fertility.

Egg Freezing
Egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation) involves retrieving and freezing unfertilized eggs to preserve fertility for potential future use in cancer patients.<SEP>Egg freezing (oocyte cryopreservation) is a procedure to preserve unfertilized eggs by freezing them, allowing for future use in assisted reproductive technologies.<SEP>Egg freezing (oocyte preservation) is a fertility preservation method involving the removal, freezing, and storage of unfertilized eggs for future use.

Ovarian Transposition
Ovarian Transposition is a surgical procedure to reposition ovaries out of the radiation field, preserving fertility and hormonal function in premenopausal patients with cervical cancer.<SEP>Ovarian Transposition is a surgical procedure to reposition ovaries outside the radiation field, preserving fertility and hormonal function in premenopausal patients.<SEP>Ovarian transposition (oophoropexy) is a surgical procedure to relocate ovaries out of the radiation beam's path, preserving fertility in premenopausal patients with cervical cancer.<SEP>Ovarian transposition (oophoropexy) is a surgical procedure to reposition ovaries outside the radiation beam's path, preserving fertility and hormonal function during rectal cancer treatment.

Non-metastatic cancer
Non-metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has not spread beyond the rectum, requiring localized treatment approaches.

Early rectal cancer
Early rectal cancer is cancer detected at an early stage, often treatable with minimally invasive procedures like endoscopic submucosal dissection.

Locally advanced cancer
Locally advanced cancer refers to cancer that has progressed within the rectum but not to distant organs, necessitating surgical or combined treatment.

Polyps with cancer
Polyps with cancer are growths on the rectal lining that may develop into invasive cancer, often detected via colonoscopy.

Pedunculated polyps
Pedunculated polyps are mushroom-shaped growths on the rectal wall, often removable via polypectomy.

Sessile polyps
Sessile polyps are flat, stalkless growths on the rectal wall, more likely to recur and requiring advanced imaging for evaluation.

Malignant (cancerous) polyp
A malignant polyp is a precancerous growth that has developed into cancer, requiring surgical removal.

Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD)
ESD is a minimally invasive procedure to remove small rectal cancers confined to the mucosal layer, often curing the disease.

Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR)
EMR is a procedure used to remove early-stage rectal cancers, similar to ESD but with different technical approaches.

Transanal local excision
Transanal local excision involves removing rectal tumors through the anus, suitable for low-risk T1 tumors.

Transanal endoscopic microsurgery (TEM)
TEM is an advanced technique for removing rectal tumors higher in the rectum, using endoscopic tools for precision.

Transanal minimally invasive surgery (TAMIS)
TAMIS is a minimally invasive approach for excising rectal tumors, offering reduced recovery times compared to traditional surgery.

Transabdominal surgery
Transabdominal surgery is a more extensive procedure for removing rectal tumors that have progressed beyond localized stages.

Stage I
Stage I is a classification of cancer staging indicating the tumor has grown into the second or third (muscle) layer of the rectal wall, requiring no further treatment.

Stage II
Stage II is a classification of cancer staging indicating the tumor has grown through the rectal wall and possibly into nearby tissues or organs, requiring more treatment.

Stage III
Stage III is a classification of cancer staging indicating cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes, requiring almost always more treatment.

Kidney Cancer
Kidney Cancer is a broad category of cancers affecting the kidneys, with Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) being the most common type.<SEP>Kidney Cancer is a broad category of cancers that affect the kidneys, with Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) being the most common type.<SEP>Kidney Cancer is a type of cancer originating in the kidneys, with RCC (Renal Cell Carcinoma) as a common subtype, and information provided by the World Health Organization.<SEP>Kidney Cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the kidneys, involving the tissues of these organs and classified under renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and other subtypes.

Transabdominal Surgery
Transabdominal Surgery is a surgical category involving abdominal incisions to remove rectal tumors, lymph nodes, and surrounding tissue, with variations like Low Anterior Resection (LAR) and Abdominoperineal Resection (APR).

Colostomy
Colostomy is a procedure creating an artificial opening for stool elimination after APR, resulting in a permanent stoma on the abdomen.<SEP>Colostomy is a surgical procedure creating an opening (stoma) on the abdomen for stool to exit, often temporary or permanent after rectal surgery.<SEP>Colostomy is a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the abdomen to divert stool, often required after the removal of the anus in anal cancer treatment.<SEP>Colostomy is a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the abdomen to divert stool, often used when reconnecting the colon is not feasible after cancer removal.

Colorectal Anastomosis
Colorectal Anastomosis is a surgical procedure reconnecting the colon to the remaining rectum, allowing near-normal bowel movements after transabdominal surgery.

Colonoanal Anastomosis
Colonoanal Anastomosis is a surgical procedure connecting the colon directly to the anus, used when colorectal anastomosis is not feasible.

Abdominoperineal Resection (APR)
APR is a surgical procedure involving the removal of the anus, rectum, and surrounding tissues, often used for metastatic anal cancer treatment.<SEP>Abdominoperineal Resection (APR) is a surgical category involving removal of the rectum, anus, and surrounding tissue, requiring a permanent colostomy for stool diversion.<SEP>Abdominoperineal Resection (APR) is a surgical procedure for anal cancer that involves removing the anus, rectum, and surrounding tissues, often followed by a permanent colostomy.<SEP>Abdominoperineal resection (APR) is a radical surgical procedure to remove the anus and surrounding tissues in cases of locally progressive or recurrent anal cancer.

Oxaliplatin
Oxaliplatin is a chemotherapy drug used in rectal cancer treatment, known to cause nerve damage (neuropathy) in fingers and toes.

Irinotecan
Irinotecan is a chemotherapy drug used in rectal cancer treatment, associated with side effects like abdominal cramping, nausea, diarrhea, and hair loss.

RCC (Renal Cell Carcinoma)
RCC (Renal Cell Carcinoma) is a subtype of kidney cancer originating in the kidneys, with the World Health Organization providing information on its spread and management.

RCC
RCC (Renal Cell Carcinoma) is the most common type of kidney cancer, characterized by tumors originating in the renal tubules and often referred to as kidney cancer.

Renal Cell Carcinoma
Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) is a specific subtype of kidney cancer, with clear cell RCC being the most prevalent form, and non-clear cell RCC encompassing other variations.<SEP>Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) is the standard name for RCC, reflecting the same condition, with clear cell RCC being the most prevalent form.

Urothelial Carcinoma
Urothelial Carcinoma is a distinct type of kidney cancer that originates in the cells lining the renal pelvis and ureter, sharing features with bladder cancer.

Wilms Tumor
Wilms Tumor (nephroblastoma) is a rare kidney cancer typically occurring in young children, involving abnormal growth of kidney cells.

Renal Sarcoma
Renal Sarcoma is a rare kidney cancer that arises in the blood vessels or connective tissue of the kidney, requiring specialized treatment approaches.

Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC)
Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, characterized by tumors in the renal tubules, and includes various subtypes such as Clear Cell RCC and Non-Clear Cell RCC.<SEP>Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) is the most common type of kidney cancer, originating in renal tubules and classified into subtypes like Clear Cell RCC and Non-Clear Cell RCC.

Clear Cell RCC
Clear Cell RCC is the most common RCC subtype, characterized by pale cells under a microscope and accounting for ~70% of RCC cases.<SEP>Clear Cell RCC is the most common subtype of RCC, occurring in about 7 out of 10 people with RCC, and is identified by its pale, clear appearance under a microscope.

Non-Clear Cell RCC
Non-Clear Cell RCC is a broad category of RCC subtypes that includes types like Papillary RCC, Chromophobe RCC, and Translocation RCC, which are less common than Clear Cell RCC.<SEP>Non-Clear Cell RCC is a heterogeneous group of RCC subtypes, including Papillary RCC, Chromophobe RCC, and Translocation RCC, collectively comprising ~30% of RCC cases.

Papillary RCC
Papillary RCC is the most common subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC, characterized by long, thin finger-like growths under a microscope and accounting for about 1 out of 10 RCC cases.<SEP>Papillary RCC is the most common subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC, featuring finger-like growths under a microscope and representing ~10% of RCC cases.

Chromophobe RCC
Chromophobe RCC is a distinct Non-Clear Cell RCC subtype with larger pale cells differing from Clear Cell RCC under microscopic examination.<SEP>Chromophobe RCC is a subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC, distinguished by pale, larger cells that differ from Clear Cell RCC under microscopic examination.

Translocation RCC
Translocation RCC is a rare Non-Clear Cell RCC subtype, often diagnosed in children or young adults, characterized by unique gene fusions promoting cancer growth.<SEP>Translocation RCC is a rare subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC, often diagnosed in children or younger adults, characterized by unique gene fusions that promote cancer development.

Unclassified RCC
Unclassified RCC describes cancers that do not fit into any specific subtype or contain multiple subtypes, making classification challenging.<SEP>Unclassified RCC refers to tumors that do not fit into specific subtypes or contain multiple subtypes, complicating classification.

Collecting Duct RCC
Collecting Duct RCC is a rare Non-Clear Cell RCC subtype forming in kidney collecting ducts, often linked to genetic factors.<SEP>Collecting Duct RCC is a rare subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC that forms in the collecting ducts or tubules of the kidney.

Renal Medullary Carcinoma (RMC)
Renal Medullary Carcinoma (RMC) is a rare Non-Clear Cell RCC subtype associated with sickle cell traits and found in young African descent individuals.<SEP>Renal Medullary Carcinoma (RMC) is a rare subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC often found in young people of African descent, associated with genetic factors and sickle cell traits.

data.entity_name: Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor
data.content:
Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor
Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor is a rare hybrid subtype combining features of Clear Cell and Papillary RCC.<SEP>Clear Cell Papillary Renal Cell Tumor is a rare subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC, combining features of Clear Cell and Papillary RCC.

Fumarate Hydratase-Deficient RCC
Fumarate Hydratase-Deficient RCC is a rare Non-Clear Cell RCC subtype linked to mutations in the Fumarate Hydratase gene.<SEP>Fumarate Hydratase-Deficient RCC is a rare subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC characterized by mutations in the Fumarate Hydratase gene, leading to specific metabolic defects.

ELOC (formerly TCEB1)-Mutated RCC
ELOC (formerly TCEB1)-Mutated RCC is a rare Non-Clear Cell RCC subtype associated with TCEB1 gene mutations.<SEP>ELOC (formerly TCEB1)-Mutated RCC is a rare subtype of Non-Clear Cell RCC associated with mutations in the TCEB1 gene, contributing to tumor development.

Sarcomatoid Features
Sarcomatoid Features refer to sarcoma-like cells in RCC, indicating aggressive behavior and potential for rapid growth and metastasis.<SEP>Sarcomatoid Features refer to the presence of sarcomatoid (sarcoma-like) cells in RCC, which can occur in any RCC subtype and indicate more aggressive tumor behavior.

Histology
Histology is a classification method for gliomas based on the microscopic appearance of tumor cells, such as astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma.<SEP>Histology is the microscopic analysis of tissue samples, critical for diagnosing RCC subtypes and guiding treatment decisions.

Metastasis
Metastasis is a category describing the spread of cancer from its primary site to distant organs such as the lung or bone.<SEP>Metastasis is a category describing the spread of cancer to distant organs or tissues, a critical factor in determining cancer stages and prognosis.<SEP>Metastasis is the process by which cancer cells spread from the primary tumor to distant organs or tissues, often leading to more severe disease progression.<SEP>Metastasis is the process by which cancer spreads from the kidney to other parts of the body via blood or lymphatic systems.<SEP>Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from the primary tumor to distant organs, a critical factor in determining cancer stages and treatment plans.<SEP>Metastasis refers to the spread of cancer from the prostate to other parts of the body, such as bones or lymph nodes, and is a critical factor in staging and treatment planning.<SEP>Metastasis refers to the spread of cancer to distant organs or bones, which is evaluated in the TNM system's M classification to determine cancer stage.<SEP>The spread of cancer from its primary site to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs, often requiring biopsy and genetic analysis.<SEP>The spread of cancer to distant organs or tissues, often requiring biopsy to confirm and guide treatment strategies.

Renal Tubules
Renal Tubules are tiny kidney structures where Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) originates, responsible for filtering blood and producing urine.

Blood
Blood is a tissue composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, playing a critical role in immune function and oxygen transport.<SEP>Blood is a tissue that functions to transport oxygen and nutrients throughout the body, carry away waste, and support the immune system. It consists of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.<SEP>Blood is a vital tissue composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, responsible for transporting oxygen, nutrients, and waste, as well as supporting the immune system and clotting.<SEP>Blood is a vital tissue composed of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, responsible for transporting oxygen, nutrients, and waste, as well as supporting the immune system.

Red Blood Cells (RBCs)
Red blood cells (RBCs) are blood cells responsible for carrying oxygen from the lungs to tissues and removing carbon dioxide from the body.<SEP>Red blood cells (RBCs) are responsible for carrying oxygen throughout the body and are produced in bone marrow from hematopoietic stem cells.

Platelets (PLTs)
Platelets (PLTs) are a category of blood cells that form clots to prevent or stop bleeding.<SEP>Platelets (PLTs) are cell fragments in the blood that play a critical role in clotting and controlling bleeding.<SEP>Platelets (PLTs) are cell fragments that help control bleeding by forming clots and are produced in bone marrow from megakaryocytes.

Burkitt Leukemia
Burkitt leukemia is a rare subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) that shares similarities with Burkitt lymphoma but is treated differently due to its distinct clinical presentation.<SEP>Burkitt leukemia is a rare, rapidly growing subtype of B-cell ALL, associated with genetic abnormalities and aggressive tumor growth.

Burkitt Lymphoma
Burkitt lymphoma is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by rapid growth of B-cell lymphomas, often associated with genetic mutations and Epstein-Barr virus infections.<SEP>Burkitt lymphoma is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that shares similarities with B-cell ALL but is treated differently due to its distinct biological characteristics.

Adolescent and Young Adult (AYA)
Adolescent and young adult (AYA) refers to individuals aged 15 to 39 at the time of cancer diagnosis, a unique group requiring specialized care and treatment protocols.

Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a type of blood cancer that originates in the stem cells of bone marrow, leading to the accumulation of immature white blood cells called blasts and impairing normal blood cell production.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer originating in the bone marrow, characterized by uncontrolled white blood cell growth.<SEP>Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer that originates in the bone marrow and involves the uncontrolled growth of abnormal white blood cells.

Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia
Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL) is a rare subtype of AML characterized by a specific genetic fusion gene (PML::RARA) and requires targeted treatment approaches.

Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasm
Blastic Plasmacytoid Dendritic Cell Neoplasm (BPDCN) is an aggressive subtype of AML that originates in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, or skin and involves abnormal plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

Blasts
Blasts are a category of immature blood cells that may indicate leukemia and are monitored in blood tests.<SEP>Blasts are immature white blood cells that are central to AML pathology. Abnormal myeloblasts accumulate in the bone marrow and blood, disrupting normal blood cell production.

Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS)
Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) is a category representing a scale used to evaluate a patient's general health and ability to perform daily tasks.<SEP>The Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) is a category representing a scale used to measure a patient's overall health and functional status, often used alongside the ECOG scale in treatment planning.<SEP>The Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) is a category that measures a patient's general health and ability to perform daily tasks, used alongside the ECOG scale in treatment planning.

Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP)
The Comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) is a category of blood tests that measure substances in the blood to assess kidney and liver function.<SEP>The comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) is a category of blood test that evaluates kidney and liver function, as well as calcium levels, to detect hypercalcemia.<SEP>The comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) is a category of blood test that evaluates kidney and liver function, electrolyte levels, and other metabolic indicators, including calcium and alkaline phosphatase.

Blood clotting tests
Blood clotting tests are a category of medical tests that evaluate the body's ability to form blood clots, essential for preventing excessive bleeding.

Liver function tests (LFTs)
Liver function tests (LFTs) are a category of blood tests that assess the health and function of the liver.

HLA typing
HLA typing is a category of blood tests that determine a person's HLA type, crucial for matching donors in hematopoietic cell transplants.

Performance status (PS)
Performance status (PS) is a category that measures a patient's general fitness and ability to perform daily tasks, influencing treatment decisions.

Bone marrow tests
Bone marrow tests are a category of medical tests used to diagnose leukemia and assess bone marrow function.<SEP>Bone marrow tests, including aspirate and biopsy, are used to evaluate bone marrow health and detect abnormalities in cancer patients.

Coagulopathy
Coagulopathy is a category of disorders characterized by impaired blood clotting, commonly associated with leukemia.

Differential
Differential is a category of blood tests that analyze white blood cell counts and their balance, aiding in diagnosing conditions like leukemia.<SEP>Differential refers to the analysis of white blood cell types in a CBC, helping identify abnormal cell populations in CLL.

CBC measurements
CBC measurements are a category of blood tests that assess hemoglobin, platelets, absolute neutrophil count (ANC), and blasts to evaluate blood health.

Hemoglobin (Hgb)
Hemoglobin (Hgb) is a category of blood measurement that indicates oxygen-carrying capacity and the need for red blood cell transfusions.

Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC)
Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) is a category of blood measurement that assesses the body's ability to fight bacterial infections.

Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) is a category of enzyme that is released by dying cells, including tumor cells, and is measured in blood tests.

Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) is a category of waste product filtered by the kidneys, with elevated levels indicating impaired kidney function.

Creatinine
Creatinine is a category of waste product produced in muscles, filtered by the kidneys, and used to assess kidney function.

Electrolytes
Electrolytes are a category of ions or particles with electrical charges that regulate fluid balance and muscle function.

Iron
Iron is a category of mineral essential for hemoglobin production, with deficiencies or excesses impacting blood health.

Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency is a category of condition characterized by insufficient iron levels, leading to anemia and fatigue.

Iron overload
Iron overload is a category of condition marked by excessive iron accumulation, potentially damaging organs like the liver.

Coagulation panel
Coagulation panel is a category of blood tests that evaluate clotting factors and diagnose coagulation disorders.

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)
Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is a category of severe coagulation disorder involving widespread clot formation and bleeding.

Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT)
Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT) is a category of treatment involving stem cell transplantation from a donor to treat blood disorders.

Fertility preservation
Fertility preservation is a category of medical strategy to maintain reproductive options during cancer treatment.

Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group
Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is an organization that defines the ECOG Performance Status (PS) scale, which assesses a patient's general health and activity level.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is an organization that develops a PS scale used to assess the general health of patients with cancer.<SEP>The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) is an organization that develops the PS scale used to assess patient health in cancer treatment.

Karnofsky Performance Status
The Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) is a scale used to evaluate a patient's functional status and overall health in cancer contexts.<SEP>The Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) is a scale used to evaluate a patient's functional status and overall health in the context of cancer treatment.

Bone Marrow Aspirate
Bone marrow aspirate is a medical procedure where liquid bone marrow is extracted using a hollow needle to analyze cells for diagnostic purposes.<SEP>Bone marrow aspirate is a procedure extracting liquid marrow for diagnostic analysis of blood cancers.

Bone Marrow Biopsy
A bone marrow biopsy involves extracting a core sample of marrow to analyze for abnormal cell proliferation, commonly used in diagnosing CLL.<SEP>A bone marrow biopsy involves extracting marrow samples to check for cancer cell presence, particularly in suspected lymphoma cases.<SEP>Bone marrow biopsy is a medical procedure involving the removal of a small piece of bone marrow tissue to assess cellular abnormalities, often used in diagnosing leukemia.<SEP>Bone marrow biopsy is a procedure removing bone tissue samples to diagnose and analyze leukemia.

Genetic Changes
Genetic changes refer to DNA mutations or chromosomal abnormalities critical in leukemia development and classification.<SEP>Genetic changes refer to mutations or abnormalities in DNA that contribute to the development and classification of leukemia, often detected through molecular testing.

Translocation
Translocation is a chromosomal abnormality where segments swap between chromosomes, commonly observed in leukemia.<SEP>Translocation is a type of genetic abnormality where parts of chromosomes break and exchange, commonly observed in leukemia and affecting cell function.

Point Mutation
Point mutation is a genetic change involving a single nucleotide alteration, potentially contributing to leukemia progression.<SEP>Point mutation is a genetic change where a single nucleotide in DNA is altered, potentially leading to the development of leukemia or affecting its progression.

Deletion
Deletion is a genetic change where DNA or chromosomal segments are missing, associated with leukemia subtypes.<SEP>Deletion is a genetic change where a segment of DNA or a chromosome is missing, contributing to the pathogenesis of certain leukemia subtypes.

Insertion
Insertion is a genetic change where an extra segment of DNA is added, potentially disrupting normal cellular function and contributing to leukemia.<SEP>Insertion is a genetic change where extra DNA segments are added, disrupting normal cellular function in leukemia.

Inversion
Inversion is a chromosomal abnormality where segments are reversed, linked to specific leukemia subtypes.<SEP>Inversion is a genetic abnormality where a segment of a chromosome is reversed, often associated with specific leukemia subtypes and their molecular profiles.

Amplification
Amplification is a genetic change where DNA segments are duplicated, increasing protein production in leukemia.<SEP>Amplification is a genetic change where a portion of a chromosome or gene is duplicated, leading to increased production of specific proteins and contributing to leukemia.

Gene Rearrangement
Gene rearrangement is a chromosomal abnormality involving DNA segment reordering, critical for leukemia classification.<SEP>Gene rearrangement is a genetic abnormality involving the reordering of DNA segments, often observed in leukemia and influencing treatment strategies.

AML Mutation Testing
AML mutation testing involves analyzing genetic and chromosomal abnormalities in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells using methods like karyotype, FISH, NGS, and PCR to guide treatment decisions.<SEP>AML mutation testing involves methods like karyotype, FISH, NGS, and PCR to identify genetic abnormalities in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells, guiding treatment decisions.

Genetic Testing Methods
Genetic testing methods encompass techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), karyotype analysis, next-generation sequencing (NGS), and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to detect chromosomal and genetic abnormalities in leukemia cells.

FISH
FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) is a technique using fluorescent probes to identify specific chromosomal abnormalities in leukemia cells, particularly useful for known genetic changes in blood or bone marrow samples.<SEP>FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) is a technique using special dyes to detect chromosomal abnormalities in leukemia cells, particularly useful for known genetic changes and applicable to blood or bone marrow samples.<SEP>FISH (Fluorescence in situ hybridization) is a DNA testing method using probes to detect genetic abnormalities in cancer cells.<SEP>Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a genetic testing category used to detect chromosomal abnormalities, such as the 17p deletion, in CLL cells to guide treatment decisions.<SEP>Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a molecular diagnostic category used to detect genetic abnormalities, such as chromosome deletions, in CLL cells.

NGS
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a high-resolution DNA analysis method that identifies mutations affecting gene function, surpassing traditional methods in detecting subtle genetic changes in leukemia-related genes.<SEP>Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a high-resolution method to analyze DNA sequences, identifying mutations that affect gene function and may be missed by other testing methods.

PCR
PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies DNA or RNA to detect minute genetic abnormalities, enabling sensitive detection of mutations and aiding in treatment response monitoring.<SEP>PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies DNA or RNA to detect minute genetic abnormalities, enabling sensitive identification of mutations and supporting treatment response monitoring in leukemia management.<SEP>PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) amplifies DNA to detect mutations, often used to generate samples for next-generation sequencing.

Hypomethylating Agents
Hypomethylating agents (e.g., Azacitidine) reverse DNA methylation, reactivating genes to promote normal cell maturation in leukemia.

Cytarabine
Cytarab, a key chemotherapy drug, is used in various regimens to treat AML, with dosing tailored to individual patient needs.<SEP>Cytarabine is a chemotherapy drug that may be used as an alternative to high-dose methotrexate in the treatment of primary CNS lymphoma.<SEP>Cytarabine is a key chemotherapy drug used in various regimens to treat AML, with dosing tailored to individual patient needs.

Methotrexate
Methotrexate is a chemotherapy drug commonly used in high doses to treat primary CNS lymphoma, though it carries risks of organ damage and requires careful monitoring.<SEP>Methotrexate is a chemotherapy drug commonly used to treat primary CNS lymphoma, inhibiting cancer cell growth.<SEP>Methotrexate is an antimetabolite used in AML treatment, particularly for intrathecal chemotherapy to target the central nervous system.

Azacitidine
Azacitidine is a hypomethylating agent that inhibits DNA methylation, helping to reactivate genes in leukemic cells.

Multidisciplinary Team (MDT)
A multidisciplinary team (MDT) is a group of healthcare professionals from diverse backgrounds collaborating to plan and implement AML treatment.

BCR::ABL1
BCR::ABL1 is a fused gene created by the translocation of chromosome 9 and chromosome 22, which is the genetic abnormality responsible for Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML).

Hypomethylating Agents (HMAs)
Hypomethylating agents are a class of drugs that block methyl groups from binding to DNA, reactivating silenced genes to allow leukemic blasts to mature into normal cells.

Azacitidine (Vidaza)
Azacitidine is a hypomethylating agent used in the treatment of leukemia, which works by inhibiting DNA methylation and reactivating tumor suppressor genes.

Decitabine (Dacogen)
Decitabine is a hypomethylating agent that inhibits DNA methylation, helping to reactivate genes that may be silenced in leukemic cells.

Gemtuzumab Ozogamicin (GO)
Gemtuzumab ozogamicin is a targeted therapy drug linked to a chemotherapy agent, which binds to CD33 proteins on leukemic blasts and delivers chemotherapy inside the cell.

FLT3 Mutations
FLT3 mutations are genetic abnormalities in the FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 gene, which are associated with certain subtypes of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and influence treatment strategies.

FLT3-ITD
FLT3-ITD (FLT3 Internal Tandem Duplication) is a specific type of FLT3 mutation characterized by a duplicated segment of DNA in the FLT3 gene, commonly found in AML cases.

Core Binding Factor (CBF)
Core Binding Factor is a genetic abnormality involving mutations in the CBFβ-MYH11 gene, which leads to a shortage of mature blood cells and is associated with certain subtypes of AML.

Hematopoietic Stem Cells
Hematopoietic stem cells are early blood-forming cells in bone marrow that give rise to all types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

White Blood Cells (WBCs)
White blood cells (WBCs) are part of the immune system, fighting infections by including granulocytes, monocytes, and lymphocytes.

Neutrophils
Neutrophils are a type of granulocyte white blood cell that defends the body against bacterial infections.

Eosinophils
Eosinophils are granulocytes involved in immune responses, particularly against parasitic infections and in allergic reactions.

Basophils
Basophils are granulocytes that release histamine and other mediators during allergic reactions and immune responses.

FLT3-TKD
FLT3-TKD (FLT3 Tyrosine Kinase Domain) is another type of FLT3 mutation involving a substitution in the tyrosine kinase domain, contributing to the development of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).

BCR::ABL1 gene
The BCR::ABL1 gene is an abnormal gene formed when parts of chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 break and trade places, leading to the Philadelphia chromosome and causing uncontrolled blood cell growth in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML).

Philadelphia chromosome
The Philadelphia chromosome is a shortened chromosome 22 resulting from the fusion of parts of chromosome 9 and 22, which is a hallmark of CML and directly linked to the BCR::ABL1 gene's activity.

Testing
Testing refers to diagnostic procedures used to identify CML, determine treatment plans, and monitor disease progression through blood tests, bone marrow tests, and genetic analysis.

Blast phase CML
Blast phase CML (BP-CML) is an advanced form of CML characterized by increased lymphoid or myeloid progenitor cells, affecting treatment options.

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a type of blood cancer that affects lymphoid progenitor cells, leading to the overproduction of abnormal lymphoblasts in the bone marrow.

Adolescents and Young Adults (AYAs)
AYAs are patients aged 15 to 39 years diagnosed with ALL, who may receive treatment in pediatric or adult centers depending on their condition.

Types of treatments
Types of treatments discusses standard therapies like steroids, chemotherapy, and systemic therapies for ALL, along with clinical trial options.

Supportive care
Supportive care covers side effects management and care strategies for patients undergoing ALL treatment.<SEP>Supportive care includes hospice care, pain management, and emotional support for patients with metastatic cancer, aiming to improve comfort and quality of life.<SEP>Supportive care is a key component of cancer care, focusing on managing symptoms and improving quality of life for patients.

BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL
BCR::ABL1-negative or BCR::ABL1-like B-ALL refers to a specific subtype of B-cell ALL requiring clinical trial-based treatment.

BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL
BCR::ABL1-positive B-ALL is a subtype of ALL treated with intensive systemic therapies targeting the BCR::ABL1 gene.

Infant ALL
Infant ALL is a distinct ALL type requiring specialized treatment approaches tailored for children under 12 months.

Pancreatic cancer
Pancreatic cancer is a separate malignancy discussed in the text, focusing on its causes, stages, and treatment advancements.<SEP>Pancreatic cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the pancreas, often requiring multidisciplinary approaches for diagnosis and treatment.

Stages of Pancreatic Cancer
The stages of pancreatic cancer range from stage 0 to stage 4, describing the progression of the disease based on tumor size and spread.

Hereditary Conditions
Hereditary conditions, such as Hereditary Breast-Ovarian Cancer Syndrome (HBOC), Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome, increase the risk of pancreatic cancer through genetic mutations.

Treatment Options
Treatment options for pancreatic cancer include surgery, drug therapy, clinical trials, and supportive care, tailored to the patient's stage and overall health.

Genetic Tests
Genetic Tests analyze DNA to identify inherited mutations that may increase cancer risk, particularly for conditions like hereditary prostate cancer.<SEP>Genetic Tests are diagnostic procedures used to identify inherited genetic mutations that may increase the risk of developing prostate cancer or influence treatment responses.<SEP>Genetic tests identify inherited mutations linked to hereditary conditions that elevate pancreatic cancer risk, such as HBOC and familial melanoma syndrome.

Multidisciplinary Team
A multidisciplinary team of specialists collaborates to develop personalized treatment plans for pancreatic cancer patients.

Pancreatic Adenocarcinomas
Pancreatic adenocarcinomas originate from exocrine cells in the pancreas and are the primary focus of treatment and research.

Hereditary Pancreatitis
Hereditary pancreatitis is a genetic condition that increases the risk of developing pancreatic cancer due to chronic inflammation.

Prostate cancer
Prostate cancer is a common malignancy in males, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth in the prostate gland, with varying symptoms and treatment options.<SEP>Prostate cancer is a type of cancer originating in the prostate gland, discussed in detail with its symptoms, causes, risk factors, and treatment options.<SEP>Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the prostate gland and is discussed in detail, including its symptoms, causes, and risk factors.

Multidisciplinary consult
A multidisciplinary consult is a collaborative meeting involving specialists to evaluate and plan treatment for complex conditions like pancreatic cancer.

Consult meeting
A consult meeting is a structured discussion among healthcare providers to review a patient's case, tests, and treatment options.

Diagnostic radiologist
A Diagnostic radiologist is a medical professional specializing in interpreting imaging tests to diagnose and monitor diseases.

Interventional radiologist
An Interventional radiologist performs minimally invasive procedures using imaging guidance to treat various medical conditions.<SEP>An interventional radiologist is a medical professional who performs minimally invasive procedures, such as core needle biopsies, using imaging guidance to diagnose and treat conditions.

Gastroenterologist
A Gastroenterologist specializes in diagnosing and treating disorders of the digestive system, including the pancreas.

Medical oncologist
A Medical oncologist specializes in cancer treatment using chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies.

Surgical oncologist
A Surgical oncologist focuses on surgically removing cancerous tumors and managing cancer-related surgical interventions.

Radiation oncologist
A Radiation oncologist uses radiation therapy to treat cancer, targeting malignant cells while minimizing damage to healthy tissue.

Geriatrician
A Geriatrician specializes in the care of elderly patients, addressing age-related health conditions and treatment complexities.

Registered dietitian
A Registered dietitian provides nutritional guidance and support to patients, particularly those with cancer-related dietary needs.

Genetic counselor
A Genetic counselor helps patients understand genetic risks, inheritance patterns, and the implications of genetic mutations for cancer.

Palliative care provider
A Palliative care provider focuses on relieving symptoms and improving quality of life for patients with serious illnesses like cancer.

Mental health provider
A Mental health provider offers psychological and emotional support to patients and families dealing with cancer diagnosis and treatment.

Jaundice
Jaundice is a condition characterized by yellowing of the skin and eyes, often caused by liver or pancreatic dysfunction.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland, often confused with prostate cancer due to similar symptoms.<SEP>Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland, which can cause urinary symptoms similar to prostate cancer.

Blood tests
Blood tests are a category of diagnostic procedures that assess organ function, disease markers, and blood composition, including complete blood counts (CBC) and comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP).<SEP>Blood tests are a category of diagnostic procedures that check for signs of disease and organ function, including complete blood counts (CBC) and comprehensive metabolic panels (CMP).<SEP>Blood tests are diagnostic procedures used to analyze blood samples for indicators of disease, including cancer markers and organ function.<SEP>Blood tests are diagnostic procedures used to analyze blood samples for signs of cancer or related conditions, such as H. pylori infection.

Genetic tests for inherited mutations
Genetic tests for inherited mutations identify genetic predispositions to cancer, aiding in risk assessment and personalized treatment planning.

Biomarker tests for profiling
Biomarker tests for profiling analyze biological markers in tissues or blood to characterize cancer characteristics and guide targeted therapies.

Endoscopic tests
Endoscopic tests involve using flexible tubes with cameras to examine internal organs, often used to detect and biopsy pancreatic abnormalities.

Multidisciplinary team
A multidisciplinary team is a collaborative group of healthcare professionals from various specialties working together to provide comprehensive cancer care.

Prostate Cancer
A type of cancer originating in the prostate gland, characterized by its association with genetic, racial, and lifestyle factors, and its progression from early-stage to advanced-stage forms.<SEP>A type of cancer originating in the prostate gland, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth, and detectable through biopsies, imaging, and genetic testing.<SEP>A type of cancer originating in the prostate gland, which may metastasize to lymph nodes, bones, or internal organs and is often managed with biopsies and genetic testing.<SEP>Prostate Cancer is a malignancy of the prostate gland, often detected through PSA testing, digital rectal exams, and imaging.<SEP>Prostate Cancer is a type of cancer that affects the prostate gland and is the central focus of the text, discussed in terms of diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis.<SEP>Prostate Cancer is a type of cancer that develops in the prostate gland. Risk assessment involves factors like PSA level, Gleason score, Grade Group, and biopsy results to determine treatment strategies.<SEP>Prostate Cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the prostate gland and is discussed in terms of its causes, risk factors, stages, and treatment options.<SEP>Prostate Cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the prostate gland and is often associated with germline mutations and biomarker testing for risk assessment and treatment planning.<SEP>Prostate Cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the prostate gland, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth and the potential to spread to other parts of the body.<SEP>Prostate cancer is a type of cancer affecting the prostate gland, often detected and monitored using various imaging and biopsy techniques.<SEP>Prostate cancer is a type of cancer originating in the prostate gland, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth and the potential for metastasis to other body parts.<SEP>Prostate cancer is a type of cancer originating in the prostate gland, discussed in the context of diagnostic imaging, treatment planning, and monitoring for recurrence.<SEP>Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the prostate gland and is often managed with hormone therapies such as androgen deprivation therapy (ADT).<SEP>Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the prostate gland, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth and the potential for metastasis.

Early-Stage Prostate Cancer
Cancer confined to the prostate gland, growing slowly and remaining localized, often termed 'localized prostate cancer' or 'early-stage cancer'.<SEP>Early-Stage Prostate Cancer refers to cancer that has not spread beyond the prostate gland and is often slow-growing and localized.

Advanced-Stage Prostate Cancer
Advanced-Stage Prostate Cancer describes cancer that has spread outside the prostate to other areas of the body, such as lymph nodes, bones, or organs.<SEP>Advanced-Stage Prostate Cancer refers to cancer that has metastasized beyond the prostate gland to other areas of the body, requiring specialized treatment approaches.<SEP>Cancer that has metastasized beyond the prostate to distant organs or lymph nodes, characterized by rapid progression and aggressive behavior.

Aggressive Prostate Cancer
Aggressive Prostate Cancer is a term used to describe cancer that grows or spreads more rapidly than average, often requiring more intense treatment.

Prostate Gland
The Prostate Gland is an organ in the male reproductive system that produces semen and contains muscles that aid in ejaculation.

Urethra
The Urethra is a tube that carries urine from the bladder and is wrapped around by the prostate gland.<SEP>The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. It is part of the urinary tract and can be affected by bladder cancer.

Bladder
An organ that stores urine, anatomically positioned beneath the prostate and involved in urinary function.<SEP>The Bladder is an organ that stores urine and is connected to the urethra.<SEP>The bladder is the organ where urothelial cancer originates and where cancer staging and grading are determined based on the depth of invasion.

Seminal Vesicles
Glands that produce a component of semen, located above the prostate and behind the bladder, contributing to reproductive physiology.<SEP>Seminal Vesicles are glands that contribute to the production of semen along with the prostate gland.

Semen
Semen is a fluid composed of secretions from the prostate, seminal vesicles, and sperm from the testicles, released during ejaculation.

PSA
PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen) is a protein produced by the prostate gland that is used as a biomarker for prostate health and cancer detection.<SEP>PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is a blood test measuring levels of a protein produced by the prostate, with elevated levels indicating potential cancer risk or disease progression.

Diet and Lifestyle
Diet and Lifestyle factors, such as high-fat diets and obesity, are linked to increased risks of prostate cancer and its aggressiveness.<SEP>Factors such as high-fat diets, smoking, and obesity associated with increased prostate cancer risk, while fruits/vegetables may reduce advanced disease risk.

Exercise and Weight
Exercise and Weight management are associated with reduced aggressiveness of prostate cancer and lower risks of mortality.

Smoking and Obesity
Smoking and Obesity are risk factors that increase the likelihood of developing and dying from prostate cancer.

Health Care Providers
Health Care Providers are professionals involved in breast cancer care, including breast specialists, radiologists, gynecologists, and lactation consultants.<SEP>Health Care Providers are professionals involved in diagnosing, screening, and treating prostate cancer, particularly for high-risk populations like Black males.

prostate cancer
Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that develops in the prostate gland, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth. It can be classified into localized and metastatic stages, with localized remaining within the prostate and metastatic spreading to other areas of the body.

PSA test
PSA test is a blood test that measures the amount of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in the bloodstream, which can indicate the presence of prostate cancer or its progression.

digital rectal exam
Digital rectal exam is a physical examination where a healthcare provider checks the prostate gland for abnormalities by inserting a gloved, lubricated finger into the rectum.

active surveillance
Active surveillance is a management approach for early-stage prostate cancer where patients undergo regular monitoring without immediate treatment, avoiding potential side effects of therapy.

hormone therapy
Hormone therapy is a treatment for prostate cancer that reduces testosterone levels to slow cancer growth, commonly used for advanced-stage disease.

surgery

Gleason score

Hysterectomy

Minimally Invasive Surgery

Quitting Smoking
Quitting Smoking is a preventive measure to reduce the risk of bladder cancer, as smoking is a major risk factor for the disease.<SEP>Quitting smoking is a health behavior that can improve cancer treatment outcomes, with support available for individuals seeking to stop smoking.

Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) is a radiation treatment category that uses precise beams to target cancer cells, commonly recommended for anal cancer.<SEP>Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) is an advanced form of EBRT that uses multiple beams to target cancer precisely, minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue.<SEP>Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) is an advanced radiation technique using multiple beams to target cancer precisely, minimizing damage to healthy tissue.

Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT)
SBRT is a specialized radiation therapy technique used for limited metastases, delivering high-dose radiation precisely to tumors while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue.<SEP>SBRT is a specialized radiation therapy used for limited metastases, delivering high-dose radiation precisely to tumors.<SEP>Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SB, a highly focused form of EBRT that delivers precise radiation doses over a few sessions, targeting tumors in the liver, lungs, or bones.<SEP>Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT) is a highly focused form of EBRT that delivers precise radiation doses over a few sessions, targeting tumors in the liver, lungs, or bones.<SEP>Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT) is a specialized form of EBRT used for metastatic cervical cancer, delivering high doses in fewer sessions to tumors in the liver, lungs, or bones.<SEP>Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy (SBRT) is a specialized radiation approach for metastatic cervical cancer, delivering high doses in fewer sessions to tumors in the liver, lungs, or bones.

Laparoscopic Surgical Staging

Pelvic Lymph Nodes
Pelvic Lymph Nodes are anatomical structures in the pelvic region commonly removed during cervical cancer treatment to assess cancer spread and guide therapy.<SEP>Pelvic Lymph Nodes are anatomical structures in the pelvic region that are commonly removed during cervical cancer treatment to assess cancer spread and guide therapy.

Para-Aortic Lymph Nodes are abdominal lymph nodes that may be removed during cervical cancer treatment if cancer has spread beyond the pelvic region.<SEP>Para-Aortic Lymph Nodes are lymph nodes in the abdomen that may be removed during cervical cancer treatment if cancer has spread beyond the pelvic region.

Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT)
Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT) is a hormone treatment to alleviate symptoms of early menopause caused by radiation therapy or ovarian removal.<SEP>Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT) is a type of hormone therapy used to alleviate symptoms of early menopause induced by radiation therapy or ovarian removal.

Survivorship encompasses long-term care and support for cancer patients, addressing treatment-related side effects and quality of life considerations.<SEP>Survivorship encompasses long-term care, monitoring for recurrence, and managing health after cancer treatment.<SEP>Survivorship encompasses ongoing care and monitoring for cancer survivors, including surveillance testing and symptom management.<SEP>Survivorship encompasses the ongoing care and support for cancer survivors, including regular surveillance testing and management of long-term effects.<SEP>Survivorship encompasses the physical, emotional, and social aspects of life after anal cancer treatment, including follow-up care and lifestyle adjustments.<SEP>Survivorship refers to the care and support provided to cancer survivors, encompassing physical, emotional, and financial aspects of life after treatment, including managing long-term side effects and maintaining health.<SEP>Survivorship refers to the care and support provided to cancer survivors, encompassing physical, emotional, and financial aspects of life after treatment.<SEP>Survivorship refers to the long-term care and support for cancer patients, including managing treatment-related side effects and quality of life considerations.

Brachytherapy

HDR Brachytherapy

LDR Brachytherapy
LDR (Low Dose-Rate) Brachytherapy involves delivering a lower dose of radiation over a longer period, often used for more advanced cervical cancers requiring extended treatment sessions.

Intracavitary Brachytherapy
Intracavitary Brachytherapy is a brachytherapy method where radioactive sources are placed inside body cavities (e.g., uterus, vagina) to target the tumor directly, often using an applicator like the tandem and ring system.

Interstitial Brachytherapy
Interstitial Brachytherapy is a specialized brachytherapy technique where radioactive material is placed directly into the tumor or adjacent tissues, typically used for advanced cancers involving the parametrium.

Tandem and Ring Applicator
The Tandem and Ring Applicator is a device used in HDR Brachytherapy to position radioactive sources within the cervix and uterus, enabling precise radiation delivery.

Tandem and Ovoid Applicator

Cancer Treatment Options refer to the various therapeutic approaches available for bladder cancer, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy, and targeted therapies.<SEP>Cancer treatment options encompass various therapeutic approaches, including surgery, radiation therapy, systemic therapy, and clinical trials, tailored to specific cancer types and stages.

Locally Advanced Cancer

Metastatic Cancer
Metastatic Cancer is a category of cancer that has spread to other parts of the body, such as bone, and behaves differently from primary cancers.<SEP>Metastatic Cancer refers to cancer that has spread to areas far from the neck, such as the lungs, liver, muscles, bones, brain, and spinal cord.<SEP>Metastatic cancer is cancer that has spread from its original site to other organs, such as the liver, lungs, or bones, making it more challenging to treat.<SEP>Metastatic cancer is cancer that has spread to distant organs, often requiring systemic therapies like chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.<SEP>Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original site, such as stage IV anal cancer, requiring aggressive treatment approaches like immunotherapy or chemoradiation.<SEP>Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original site, such as stage IV anal cancer, requiring aggressive treatment approaches.
