data.content:
Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Cervix (NECC)
NECC is a rare, aggressive subtype of cervical cancer requiring distinct treatment approaches compared to squamous cell carcinoma.<SEP>Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Cervix (NECC) is a rare, aggressive subtype of cervical cancer with neuroendocrine features.<SEP>Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Cervix (NECC) is a specific subtype of cervical cancer characterized by neuroendocrine features.

Lymphovascular Space Invasion (LVSI)
LVSI is a pathological feature indicating cancer spread into blood vessels or lymphatics, influencing treatment decisions.

PD-L1 Expression
PD-L1 Expression is a biomarker indicating potential responsiveness to immunotherapies in recurrent cervical cancer.<SEP>PD-L1 Expression is a biomarker indicating potential responsiveness to immunotherapies in recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer.

Follow-up Visits
Follow-up Visits are scheduled medical check-ups after treatment to monitor for recurrence, involving physical exams and imaging.<SEP>Follow-up Visits are scheduled medical check-ups post-treatment to monitor for recurrence, involving physical exams, imaging, and blood tests.

Exploratory Surgery
Exploratory Surgery is performed to determine the extent of cancer spread and guide treatment decisions for recurrent cervical cancer.

Molecular Testing
Molecular Testing analyzes genetic mutations or proteins in tumors to inform targeted therapies and treatment options.<SEP>Molecular Testing analyzes genetic or protein markers in tumors to guide targeted therapies and treatment strategies.

Genomic Testing
Genomic Testing examines the genetic makeup of tumors to identify mutations that may guide treatment decisions.

Comprehensive Genomic Profiling (CGP)
Comprehensive Genomic Profiling (CGP) provides a detailed analysis of tumor genetics to identify actionable mutations.

Tumor Gene Testing
Tumor Gene Testing evaluates genetic changes in cancer cells to guide personalized treatment strategies.

NTRK Gene Fusion
NTRK Gene Fusion is a genetic alteration in tumors that may indicate eligibility for targeted therapies.<SEP>NTRK Gene Fusion is a genetic mutation that can be targeted with specific therapies for thyroid cancer.

HER2 RET Gene Fusion
HER2 RET Gene Fusion refers to specific genetic fusions in tumors that may guide targeted treatment approaches.

Pelvic Exenter
Pelvic Exenter is a surgical procedure to remove pelvic organs affected by localized cervical cancer recurrence.<SEP>Pelvic Exenter is a surgical procedure to remove pelvic organs affected by recurrent cervical cancer, often considered for localized recurrence.

Physical Exams
Physical Exams are conducted during follow-up visits to assess new or worsening symptoms indicative of cancer recurrence.

Pap Tests
Pap Tests screen for abnormal or precancerous cells in the cervix, though less effective at detecting recurrent cervical cancer.

Pelvic Exenteration Surgery
Pelvic exenteration surgery is a radical procedure involving the removal of multiple pelvic organs to cure cancer by eliminating all affected tissues.

Ablative Therapies
Ablative therapies are localized treatments that destroy cancerous lesions with minimal damage to surrounding healthy tissue, often using specialized needles or radiation.

Metastatic cervical cancer
Metastatic cervical cancer is a type of cancer that is usually treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy, depending on biomarkers like PD-L1 and TMB-H.

Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL)
Mediastinal gray zone lymphoma is a type of lymphoma with overlapping features of primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and Hodgkin lymphoma (HL), typically treated with chemotherapy.

Hodgkin lymphoma (HL)
Hodgkin lymphoma is a type of lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, which are large, abnormal lymphocytes.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is a broad category of lymphomas that includes various subtypes, such as primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL) and gray zone lymphomas.

Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBL)
Primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that differs from mediastinal gray zone lymphoma (MGZL) in treatment approaches and clinical features.

DLBCL-NOS
DLBCL-NOS (Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma, not otherwise specified) is a lymphoma classification for cancers found outside the mediastinum, typically treated with chemotherapy and possibly rituximab.<SEP>DLBCL-NOS (Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma, not otherwise specified) is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that includes disease found outside the mediastinum.

Clinical trial
Clinical trials are research studies that may offer patients access to new treatments and are often recommended for patients with certain biomarkers or treatment-resistant cancers.

PD-L1 biomarker
PD-L1 biomarker is a protein expressed on cancer cells that indicates responsiveness to immunotherapy, particularly pembrolizumab (Keytruda).

TMB-H biomarker
TMB-H (Tumor Mutational Burden-High) biomarker indicates a high number of genetic mutations in cancer cells, making them more responsive to immunotherapy.

MSI-H/dMMR biomarker
MSI-H/dMMR (Microsatellite Instability-High/Deficient Mismatch Repair) biomarker indicates genetic instability in cancer cells, making them responsive to immunotherapy.

Tisotumab vedotin-tftv (Tivdak)
Tisotumab vedotin-tftv (Tivdak) is a targeted therapy used for cancers without specific biomarkers, particularly in advanced stages.

Cemiplimab (Libtayo)
Cemiplimab (Libtayo) is an immunotherapy option for cancers with specific biomarkers or as a second-line treatment.

Pembrolizumab (Keytruda)
Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) is an immune checkpoint inhibitor used for cancers with PD-L1–positive or TMB-H biomarkers.<SEP>Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) is an immunotherapy drug used to treat cancers with MSI-H/dMMR or TMB-H characteristics, leveraging the immune system to target tumor cells.

Topotecan
Topotecan is a chemotherapy drug used in combination with other agents for treating metastatic cervical cancer.

MGZL
MGZL (Mediastinal Gray Zone Lymphoma) is a rare type of lymphoma with features of both classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) and non-Hodgkin PMBL, presenting treatment challenges due to lack of standard protocols.

Thyroid Cancer
A type of cancer originating in the thyroid gland, characterized by uncontrolled cell growth. It includes various subtypes such as papillary, follicular, and medullary thyroid cancers. Treatment options include surgery, radioactive iodine therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. Recurrence and survivorship are critical aspects of its management.<SEP>Thyroid Cancer is a category of cancers originating in the thyroid gland, which can be metastatic and require specific treatment approaches.<SEP>Thyroid Cancer is a malignancy of the thyroid gland, categorized into differentiated (e.g., papillary, follicular), medullary, and anaplastic types, each with distinct treatment approaches.<SEP>Thyroid Cancer is a medical condition involving abnormal growth of thyroid cells, often treated with hormone therapy, radioactive iodine, or radiation, depending on the cancer type and risk level.<SEP>Thyroid Cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the thyroid gland and is discussed in the text regarding treatment and follow-up.<SEP>Thyroid cancer is a type of cancer affecting the thyroid gland, often curable with surgery, and has risk factors including radiation exposure and family history.<SEP>Thyroid cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the thyroid gland, with subtypes like anaplastic thyroid cancer being particularly aggressive and requiring combination treatments like chemotherapy and radiation.

Cowden syndrome
Cowden syndrome is an inherited genetic disorder linked to follicular thyroid cancer and other cancers, often associated with mutations in the PTEN gene.

Carney complex
Carney complex is a genetic syndrome associated with thyroid cancer, characterized by multiple endocrine neoplasias and other systemic manifestations.

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN)
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) is a genetic disorder linked to thyroid cancer, involving tumors in multiple endocrine glands and requiring family history assessment.

Thyroid gland
The thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped organ in the neck responsible for producing hormones that regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and other bodily functions.

Thyroid nodules
Thyroid nodules are abnormal growths within the thyroid gland, most of which are benign, but some may indicate thyroid cancer or other conditions.

Radiation exposure
Radiation exposure is a significant risk factor for thyroid cancer, particularly from childhood treatments or environmental catastrophes.

Family history
Family history of thyroid cancer or related syndromes increases an individual's risk of developing thyroid cancer, often indicating hereditary genetic mutations.

Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is a condition characterized by excessive thyroid hormone production, which can be associated with thyroid cancer or other endocrine disorders.

TSH test
TSH test measures thyroid-stimulating hormone levels to assess thyroid function, aiding in diagnosing thyroid cancer and evaluating nodule activity.

Thyroid Nodule
A thyroid nodule is a lump or abnormal growth within the thyroid gland, often evaluated for potential cancerous characteristics through diagnostic tests and imaging.

TSH Test
The TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone) test measures thyroid hormone levels to assess nodule activity and detect hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.

RAI Uptake Test
The Radioactive Iodine (RAI) uptake test evaluates whether a thyroid nodule produces thyroid hormone, aiding in cancer risk assessment.

Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy
Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy is a treatment approach to maintain TSH levels within a therapeutic range, preventing cancer recurrence and managing metabolic balance in thyroid cancer patients.<SEP>Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy is a treatment approach to manage TSH levels in patients with thyroid cancer, preventing cancer recurrence and maintaining metabolic balance.<SEP>Thyroid Hormone Replacement Therapy is a treatment involving levothyroxine to manage hormone levels after thyroidectomy, essential for patients who have had their thyroid removed.<SEP>Thyroid hormone replacement therapy is a lifelong treatment for patients who have undergone total thyroidectomy, maintaining hormonal balance.

Papillary Carcinoma
Papillary carcinoma is the most common type of thyroid cancer, characterized by slow growth and spread, often managed with surgery and hormone therapy.

Follicular Carcinoma
Follicular carcinoma is a type of differentiated thyroid cancer that originates from thyroid follicular cells, typically growing slowly and responding well to treatment.

Oncocytic Carcinoma
Oncocytic Carcinoma is an uncommon thyroid cancer type that is more likely to spread to lymph nodes and requires thorough pathological examination.<SEP>Oncocytic Carcinoma is an uncommon thyroid cancer type that tends to spread to lymph nodes and requires detailed pathological examination for diagnosis.<SEP>Oncocytic carcinoma is a rare type of thyroid cancer with distinctive cell features, often requiring surgical intervention and further testing for malignancy.

Differentiated Thyroid Cancers
Differentiated thyroid cancers are a category of thyroid cancers that include papillary, follicular, and oncocytic carcinomas, typically growing slowly and responding well to treatment.<SEP>Differentiated thyroid cancers include papillary, follicular, and oncocytic carcinomas, which grow and spread slowly, with treatment focusing on surgery and hormone therapy.

Medullary Thyroid Cancer
Medullary thyroid cancer is a hereditary form of thyroid cancer that arises from parafollicular cells, often managed with surgery and genetic screening.

Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer
Anaplastic thyroid cancer is an aggressive, rare form of thyroid cancer that primarily affects older adults, requiring intensive treatment approaches.

Pathology Review
Pathology review involves analyzing biopsy samples under a microscope to determine whether a nodule is cancerous and identify the cancer type.

Levothyroxine
Levothyroxine is a synthetic thyroid hormone used to replace or supplement thyroid hormone in patients with hypothyroidism, particularly in managing thyroid cancer by suppressing TSH levels.<SEP>Levothyroxine is a thyroid hormone replacement therapy used to manage thyroid hormone levels in patients with thyroid cancer or hypothyroidism.

Synthroid
Synthroid is a brand-name medication containing levothyroxine, used similarly to manage thyroid hormone levels and suppress TSH in thyroid cancer patients.<SEP>Synthroid is a thyroid hormone replacement therapy similar to levothyroxine, used to regulate thyroid hormone levels in patients with thyroid disorders.

Radioactive Iodine Therapy
Radioactive Iodine Therapy (RAI) is a treatment method using iodine-131 to destroy thyroid cancer cells, particularly effective for differentiated thyroid cancers.<SEP>Radioactive Iodine Therapy (RAI) is a treatment using iodine-131 to destroy thyroid cancer cells that absorb iodine, primarily for differentiated thyroid cancers.

Thyrogen
Thyrogen is a medication used to temporarily increase TSH levels in patients undergoing radioactive iodine therapy, enabling continued thyroid hormone replacement.<SEP>Thyrogen is a synthetic hormone used to temporarily elevate TSH levels, enabling continued thyroid hormone replacement during radioactive iodine therapy.

Whole-Body RAI Scan
Whole-Body RAI Scan is a diagnostic procedure performed after radioactive iodine therapy to detect remaining thyroid tissue or cancer cells in the body.<SEP>Whole-Body RAI Scan is a diagnostic procedure performed after radioactive iodine therapy to detect residual thyroid tissue or cancer cells in the body.

Simulation
Simulation is a planning session conducted before radiation therapy to create a personalized radiation treatment plan using imaging techniques like CT scans.<SEP>Simulation is a planning session conducted before radiation therapy to create a personalized treatment plan using imaging techniques like CT scans.

Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) is a hormone produced by the pituitary gland that regulates thyroid hormone production, monitored to adjust treatment for thyroid cancer patients.

Radioactive Iodine (RAI)
Radioactive Iodine (RAI) is a radioactive form of iodine used in therapy to target and destroy thyroid cancer cells that absorb iodine, commonly used in differentiated thyroid cancers.

Thyroidectomy
Thyroidectomy is a general term for the surgical removal of the thyroid gland, which can be performed as a total thyroidectomy or lobectomy depending on the cancer's severity.<SEP>Thyroidectomy is a surgical procedure to remove all or part of the thyroid gland, often performed as a primary treatment for thyroid cancer.

Calcium and Vitamin D Supplements
Calcium and Vitamin D Supplements are recommended to strengthen bones in patients undergoing thyroid hormone replacement therapy, mitigating the risk of osteoporosis.

Endocrinologist
An endocrinologist is a medical specialist who diagnoses and treats disorders of the endocrine system, including thyroid cancer.<SEP>Endocrinologist is a medical specialist who manages hormone-related conditions, including thyroid hormone replacement and TSH level monitoring in thyroid cancer patients.

Nuclear Medicine Specialist
Nuclear Medicine Specialist is a physician who uses radioactive substances, such as iodine-131, for diagnosing and treating thyroid cancer through targeted therapies.

Radiation Oncologist
A Radiation Oncologist is a medical specialist who plans and administers radiation therapy to treat cancers, including anal cancer, and manages treatment-related side effects.<SEP>A radiation oncologist is a medical doctor who specializes in using radiation therapy to treat cancer, including thyroid cancer.<SEP>A radiation oncologist plans and administers radiation therapy to target and treat cancer, often as part of a multidisciplinary approach.<SEP>Radiation Oncologist is a specialist who administers radiation therapy, such as external beam radiation, to treat thyroid cancer, particularly anaplastic variants.

Iodine-131
Iodine-131 is a radioactive isotope of iodine used in radioactive iodine therapy to target and destroy thyroid cancer cells that absorb iodine.

Thyrotropin Alfa
Thyrotropin Alfa is a synthetic hormone used to temporarily increase TSH levels, enabling continued thyroid hormone replacement during radioactive iodine therapy.

Radioactive Iodine Scan
Radioactive Iodine Scan is a diagnostic procedure using iodine-131 to visualize thyroid tissue and detect cancerous cells, often performed before or after radioactive iodine therapy.

Radiation Planning Session
Radiation Planning Session is a pre-treatment event where imaging and patient-specific data are used to design an individualized radiation therapy plan for external beam radiation.

Pituitary Gland
Pituitary Gland is an endocrine gland in the brain that produces thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), regulating thyroid hormone production and metabolic activity.

Papillary Thyroid Cancer
Papillary Thyroid Cancer is a type of differentiated thyroid cancer that is the most common form, often treated with surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.

Follicular and Oncocytic Carcinoma
Follicular and Oncocytic Carcinoma are subtypes of differentiated thyroid cancers, which may have varying growth rates and treatment approaches.

Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy
Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy is a treatment used to destroy remaining cancer cells after thyroidectomy, particularly in cases of papillary thyroid cancer.<SEP>Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy is a treatment used to destroy remaining thyroid cancer cells after surgery, particularly in cases of differentiated thyroid cancer.<SEP>Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy is a treatment used to destroy residual thyroid cancer cells after surgery, particularly for differentiated thyroid cancers like follicular or oncocytic types.

Active Surveillance
Active Surveillance is a management approach for small, low-risk thyroid cancers where the tumor is monitored without immediate surgery, using ultrasound to track its size.

Total Thyroidectomy
Total Thyroidectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the entire thyroid gland, recommended for tumors that have spread beyond the thyroid or are larger than 4 cm.<SEP>Total Thyroidectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the entire thyroid gland, typically recommended for more aggressive or spread-out thyroid cancers.

Lobectomy
Lobectomy is a surgical procedure to remove only part of the thyroid gland, considered an option for small, low-risk cancers where thyroid hormone replacement may not be necessary.<SEP>Lobectomy is a surgical procedure to remove part of the thyroid gland, often considered for less invasive cancers when the tumor is confined to the thyroid.

Nuclear Medicine Doctor
A nuclear medicine doctor specializes in using radioactive substances to diagnose and treat diseases, including thyroid cancer.

NIFTP
NIFTP (Noninvasive Follicular Thyroid Neoplasm with Papillary-Like Nuclear Features) is a low-risk, noninvasive thyroid tumor previously classified as an encapsulated follicular variant of papillary thyroid cancer.<SEP>NIFTP (Noninvasive Follicular Thyroid Neoplasm with Papillary-Like Nuclear Features) is a low-risk, noninvasive thyroid tumor previously known as the encapsulated follicular variant of papillary thyroid cancer.

Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma
Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC) is the second most common type of thyroid cancer, characterized by invasion of blood vessels and requiring surgical intervention.<SEP>Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC) is the second most common type of thyroid cancer, known for invading blood vessels and requiring surgical intervention.

Pathologic Examination
Pathologic examination is a medical procedure involving analysis of tissue samples to determine tumor malignancy, benignancy, or specific subtypes like NIFTP.<SEP>Pathologic examination is a medical procedure involving the analysis of tissue samples to determine the nature of a tumor, including whether it is benign or malignant.

Monitoring
Monitoring refers to the ongoing follow-up care and testing to track the progression of thyroid cancer and assess the effectiveness of treatment.<SEP>Monitoring refers to the ongoing follow-up care and testing to track thyroid cancer progression and assess treatment effectiveness.

Follow-Up Testing
Follow-Up Testing involves regular medical evaluations, including blood tests and imaging, to detect any recurrence of thyroid cancer after treatment.<SEP>Follow-Up Testing involves regular medical evaluations, including blood tests and imaging, to detect cancer recurrence after treatment.

RAI Therapy
RAI Therapy (Radioactive Iodine Therapy) is a treatment option for thyroid cancers that take up iodine, particularly for metastatic papillary, follicular, or oncocytic thyroid cancers.

Follow-up Care
Follow-up Care involves monitoring and testing after thyroidectomy to detect cancer recurrence, including physical exams, blood tests, and neck ultrasounds.

Neck Ultrasound
Neck Ultrasound is a diagnostic tool used to monitor for the return of thyroid cancer after treatment.

TSH Blood Test
TSH Blood Test measures thyroid-stimulating hormone levels to assess thyroid function and monitor for cancer recurrence.

Thyroglobulin (Tg)
Thyroglobulin is a protein produced by thyroid tissue; its levels in the blood can indicate the presence of cancer recurrence after thyroidectomy.

Anti-thyroglobulin Antibodies (Tg ab)
Anti-thyroglobulin Antibodies are proteins that can interfere with thyroglobulin testing, indicating a potential immune response to thyroid cancer.

Thyroid-stimulating Hormone (TSH)
Thyroid-stimulating Hormone is a hormone produced by the pituitary gland that regulates thyroid function; its levels are monitored to detect cancer recurrence.

Lenvatinib (Lenvima)
Lenvatinib (Lenvima) is a targeted therapy recommended for advanced thyroid cancer that cannot be removed with surgery and is progressing.

Sorafenib (Nexavar)
Sorafenib (Nexavar) is another targeted therapy recommended for advanced thyroid cancer that cannot be removed with surgery and is progressing.

Cabozantinib (Cabometyx)
Cabozantinib (Cabometyy) is a targeted therapy recommended if cancer progresses after treatment with Lenvatinib or Sorafenib.

ALK Gene Fusion
ALK Gene Fusion is a genetic mutation that can be targeted with specific therapies for thyroid cancer.

BRAF Gene Mutations
BRAF Gene Mutations are genetic changes that can be targeted with specific therapies for thyroid cancer.

RET Gene Fusion
RET Gene Fusion is a genetic mutation found in some medullary thyroid cancers and can be targeted with specific therapies.

Mismatch Repair Deficiency
Mismatch Repair Deficiency is a genetic feature that can be targeted with specific therapies for thyroid cancer.

Tumor Mutational Burden-High (TMB-H)
Tumor Mutational Burden-High (TMB-H) is a genetic feature that can be targeted with specific therapies for thyroid cancer.

Next-generation Sequencing (NGS)
Next-generation Sequencing (NGS) is a method used to test for multiple biomarkers simultaneously in thyroid cancer.

NCCN Guidelines for Patients®
An organization providing evidence-based guidelines for cancer care, including resources for rectal cancer and melanoma management.<SEP>The NCCN Guidelines for Patients® is an organization that provides trusted, expert-guided information on cancer care and treatment recommendations.

Bone Cancer
Bone Cancer is a category of cancer affecting bones, discussed in the text regarding testing, staging, and treatment options.<SEP>Bone Cancer is a category of cancer that originates in bone tissue or cartilage, including primary and secondary (metastatic) forms.<SEP>Bone Cancer is a type of cancer that affects bones, discussed in the text regarding testing, staging, and treatment options.<SEP>Bone cancer refers to malignant tumors originating in the bones, which can be staged using the TNM system to assess tumor size, spread, and prognosis.

Chondrosarcoma
Chondrosarcoma is a specific type of bone cancer discussed in the text, typically treated with surgery.<SEP>Chondrosarcoma is a type of bone cancer that originates in cartilage cells, often found in joints and other cartilage-rich areas.

Osteosarcoma
Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone tumor that arises from cells forming bone tissue, commonly affecting areas of rapid bone growth.<SEP>Osteosarcoma is the most common type of bone cancer, typically treated with a combination of therapies.

Ewing Sarcoma
Ewing Sarcoma is a rare type of bone cancer that originates in the bone marrow, often found in long bones or flat bones like the pelvis.<SEP>Ewing Sarcoma is a type of bone cancer, often treated with systemic therapy as the initial approach.

Giant Cell Tumor of Bone
Giant Cell Tumor of Bone is a benign or malignant tumor that develops in the metaphysis of bones, near growth plates.<SEP>Giant Cell Tumor of Bone is a non-cancerous condition that requires aggressive treatment to prevent bone damage.

Chordoma
Chordoma is a rare bone cancer that originates from notochordal cells, typically found in the spine or base of the skull.<SEP>Chordoma is a rare type of bone cancer, with treatment options including surgery or radiation therapy.

Soft Tissue Sarcoma
Soft Tissue Sarcoma is a category of cancers arising from soft tissues like fat, muscles, and nerves, distinct from bone sarcomas.

Multiple Myeloma
Multiple Myeloma is a type of cancer that affects plasma cells in the bone marrow, often associated with bone destruction.

Bone Tumor
Bone Tumor is a general term for abnormal growths in bone tissue, which can be benign or malignant.

Malignant
Malignant refers to cancerous tumors that grow uncontrollably and can spread to other parts of the body.

Benign
Benign refers to non-cancerous tumors that do not spread to other tissues and are typically less aggressive.

Compact Bone
Compact Bone is the dense, hard outer layer of bone tissue that provides structural support and protection.

Spongey Bone
Spongey Bone is the porous, inner layer of bone tissue containing red marrow and providing a lightweight yet strong structure.

Red Marrow
Red Marrow is the soft tissue within bones responsible for producing blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

Yellow Marrow
Yellow Marrow is the fatty tissue found in bones, primarily replacing red marrow as the body ages.

Hormonal Birth Control
Hormonal Birth Control is a method mentioned in the text to prevent pregnancy during cancer treatment.

Pregnancy test
Pregnancy tests are a category of diagnostic procedures to determine if a patient can become pregnant before starting cancer treatment, as cancer therapies can impact fertility.<SEP>Pregnancy tests are a category of diagnostic procedures used to determine if a patient can become pregnant before starting cancer treatment.

Complete blood count (CBC)
The complete blood count (CBC) is a category of blood test that measures red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets (PLTs) to assess blood health.<SEP>The complete blood count (CBC) is a category of blood test that measures red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), and platelets (PLTs) to evaluate blood health and detect abnormalities.

X-ray
X-rays are a category of imaging tests that use ionizing radiation to create images of internal structures, such as bones and organs, often referred to as radiographs.<SEP>X-rays are a category of imaging tests that use radiation to create images of internal body structures, often referred to as radiographs.

Bone scan
Bone scans are a category of imaging tests that use a radiotracer to detect bone damage, which can be caused by cancer, treatment, or other conditions, highlighting areas of abnormal activity.<SEP>Bone scans are a category of imaging tests that use a radiotracer to detect bone damage, which can be caused by cancer, treatment, or other conditions.

Genetic cancer risk testing
Genetic testing using blood or saliva identifies inherited gene mutations that increase cancer risk, aiding in family risk assessment and treatment planning.

Ewing sarcoma
Ewing sarcoma is a type of cancer characterized by specific genetic fusions, such as EWSR1-FLI1, resulting from somatic mutations during tissue development.

Cancer center
A cancer center is a specialized facility providing comprehensive cancer diagnosis, treatment, and research services, including biopsies, genetic testing, and advanced imaging.

Core needle biopsy
Core needle biopsy removes tissue samples with a hollow needle that can grab a piece of tissue, often performed under light sedation by an interventional radiologist.

Surgical biopsy
Surgical (open) biopsy removes a sample of the tumor through a small incision, requiring a trip to the operating room and performed by the treating surgeon.

Bone marrow aspirate
Bone marrow aspirate takes liquid bone marrow from the sponge-like structure of the bone, typically from the hip, to evaluate cellular abnormalities.

Bone marrow biopsy
Bone marrow biopsy removes a core sample of the sponge-like bone marrow to assess cellular and structural abnormalities.

Microsatellite instability (MSI)
Microsatellite instability (MSI) refers to errors in DNA repair mechanisms that lead to genetic mutations, often associated with certain cancers and treatment responses.

Deficient mismatch repair (dMMR)
Deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) is a condition where DNA repair errors are not corrected, leading to microsatellite instability and specific cancer vulnerabilities.

bone cancer
Bone cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the bones, characterized by abnormal cell growth and can affect various parts of the skeletal system.

microsatellite instability (MSI)
Microsatellite instability (MSI) refers to a condition where errors in DNA repair mechanisms lead to an accumulation of mutations in microsatellite regions, often associated with certain cancers.

deficient mismatch repair (dMMR)
Deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) is a genetic condition where the body's ability to correct DNA replication errors is impaired, leading to increased mutation rates and specific cancer vulnerabilities.

tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H)
Tumor mutational burden-high (TMB-H) indicates a high number of mutations per million base pairs in tumor DNA, often linked to immunotherapy responsiveness and aggressive cancer behavior.

tumor mutation testing
Tumor mutation testing is a diagnostic process that analyzes DNA mutations in cancer cells to guide treatment decisions and identify potential therapeutic targets.

next-generation sequencing (NGS)
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a high-throughput DNA sequencing technology used to detect genetic mutations and variations in tumor DNA with greater precision than traditional methods.

polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a molecular biology technique that amplifies specific DNA sequences, enabling the detection of genetic mutations and other biomarkers in cancer cells.

IDH1 mutation
IDH1 mutation refers to a specific genetic alteration in the isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 gene, commonly associated with certain types of cancers like chondrosarcoma and linked to targeted therapies.

ivosidenib (Tibsovo)
Ivosidenbed (Tibsovo) is a targeted therapy drug used to treat cancers with IDH1 mutations, particularly in chondrosarcoma patients, by inhibiting the mutated IDH1 enzyme.<SEP>Ivosidenib (Tibsovo) is a targeted therapy drug used to treat cancers with IDH1 mutations, particularly in chondrosarcoma patients, by inhibiting the mutated IDH1 enzyme.

nivolumab (Opdivo)
Nivolumab (Opdivo) is an immunotherapy drug that may be used for TMB-H tumors, working by blocking immune checkpoint proteins to enhance anti-tumor immune responses.

ipilimumab (Yervoy)
Ipilimumab (Yervoy) is an immunotherapy drug that may be used for TMB-H tumors, targeting the CTLA-4 protein to boost T-cell activation against cancer cells.

chondrosarcoma
Chondrosarcoma is a type of bone cancer that originates in cartilage cells, often associated with IDH1 mutations and treated with targeted therapies like ivosidenib.

Appendicular Skeleton
The appendicular skeleton consists of 126 bones in the upper and lower limbs, shoulder girdle, and pelvic girdle, and is a site for tumors that require specific staging criteria.

Spine
The spine, composed of 24 vertebrae, is a common location for bone tumors with distinct staging criteria based on vertebral involvement.

Pelvis
The Pelvis is the bony structure housing the anal canal and large bowel, with the anus located at its distal end.<SEP>The pelvis is a basin-shaped structure containing bones that connect the legs to the body, and tumors here are staged based on segmental involvement and spread.

CRUK
CRUK (Cancer Research UK) is an organization associated with the diagram illustrating the liver's anatomy and blood supply.

Liver Cancer
Liver Cancer is a category of cancer that originates in the liver or spreads to the liver from other organs, classified into primary and secondary types.<SEP>Liver cancer refers to cancers that originate in the liver, including primary liver cancers like HCC and secondary liver cancers that metastasize from other organs.

Grading
Grading is a category that assesses how abnormal cancer cells appear under a microscope, indicating their growth and spread potential.<SEP>Grading is a classification system used to assess the aggressiveness and growth rate of cancer cells.

Primary Liver Cancer
Primary Liver Cancer is a category of cancer that originates in the liver, including types like hepatocellular carcinoma and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.

Secondary Liver Cancer
Secondary Liver Cancer is a category of cancer that spreads to the liver from other organs, such as colon cancer metastasizing to the liver.

Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is a category of primary liver cancer, with a subtype called fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma (FLHC).<SEP>Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary liver cancer, characterized by the uncontrolled growth of liver cells.

Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma (FLHC)
Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma (FLHC) is a rare subtype of hepatocellular carcinoma, typically occurring in younger individuals.

Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma
Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma is a category of primary liver cancer that originates in the bile ducts within the liver.

Mixed-Type Tumor
Mixed-Type Tumor is a rare category of liver cancer composed of both hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma components.

Hepatobiliary System
Hepatobiliary System is a category encompassing the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts, functioning in bile production and digestion.

Digestive System
Digestive System is a category of bodily systems that includes the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and intestines, responsible for food breakdown and nutrient absorption.<SEP>The digestive system is responsible for taking in and breaking down food, absorbing nutrients, and removing waste from the body.

Cirrhosis
Cirrhosis is a chronic liver disease marked by scarring of the liver tissue, often caused by hepatitis, alcohol use, or non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

Hepatitis B virus
Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a viral infection that causes liver inflammation, which can lead to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.

Hepatitis C virus
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a viral infection that leads to chronic liver disease, increasing the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a condition characterized by fat accumulation in the liver, which can progress to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Genetic hemochromatosis
Genetic hemochromatosis is an inherited condition causing excessive iron storage in the liver, which can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.<SEP>Genetic hemochromatosis is an inherited condition causing the liver to store too much iron from food, leading to liver damage and cancer risk.

Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic disorder that results in liver damage and an increased risk of liver cancer.

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis is a chronic liver disease that causes damage to bile ducts, potentially leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Hepatitis
Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver, often caused by viral infections like hepatitis B or C, which can progress to chronic liver disease and cancer.

Hepatobiliary system
The hepatobiliary system includes the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts, and is involved in the production and transport of bile.

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) test
The alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) test is a blood test used to screen for liver cancer by measuring the level of AFP, a protein associated with liver tumors.

liver cancer
Liver cancer is a type of cancer that affects the liver and is the focus of the text. It is discussed in terms of risk factors, screening, diagnosis, and treatment.

stomach cancer
Stomach cancer is a type of cancer that affects the stomach and is discussed in the context of the digestive system and its relationship to other cancers.

digestive system
The digestive system is a collection of organs responsible for breaking down food and absorbing nutrients, including the stomach, liver, and intestines. It is central to understanding the context of stomach and liver cancers.

risk factors
Risk factors are elements that increase the likelihood of developing liver cancer, such as cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B, and other health conditions.

screening
Screening involves regular tests to detect diseases early, particularly in individuals at risk for liver cancer, with the goal of improving treatment outcomes.

diagnosis
Diagnosis refers to the process of confirming liver cancer through tests like blood tests, imaging studies, and biopsies, which inform treatment decisions.

treatment
Treatment encompasses the medical interventions used to address liver cancer, based on diagnostic findings and patient-specific factors.

family history
Family history involves the medical history of blood relatives, which can indicate a genetic predisposition to certain cancers, including liver and stomach cancers.

medical history
Medical history is a record of an individual's health issues, treatments, and conditions, which plays a role in diagnosing and managing liver cancer.

biopsy
Biopsy involves the removal and analysis of tissue samples to confirm the presence of cancer, often used in the diagnosis of liver and stomach cancers.

cirrhosis
Cirrhosis is a chronic liver disease that increases the risk of developing liver cancer, often resulting from long-term damage to the liver.

chronic hepatitis B
Chronic hepatitis B is a viral infection that can lead to liver damage and is a significant risk factor for liver cancer.

Stomach
The stomach is a part of the digestive system where food is broken down into chyme using stomach contractions and enzymes.

Esophagus
The esophagus is a muscular tube that transports food and drink from the mouth to the stomach.

Small Intestine
The small intestine is where nutrients from digested food are absorbed into the bloodstream.

Colon
The colon is part of the digestive system that absorbs water and electrolytes from the remaining food material.

Rectum
The rectum is the final section of the large intestine where feces are stored before elimination.

Gallbladder
The gallbladder stores and releases bile into the small intestine to aid in fat digestion.

Pancreas
The pancreas produces digestive enzymes and hormones that help in the breakdown of food and regulation of blood sugar.

Intestines
The intestines are the organs responsible for the majority of nutrient absorption in the digestive system.

Stomach Cancer
Stomach cancer is a type of cancer that originates in the cells lining the stomach, primarily adenocarcinomas.

My Dad
My dad is a person who was diagnosed with stomach cancer and is now clinically cured, advocating for cancer patients.

Early-stage stomach cancer
Early-stage stomach cancer has not grown beyond the first layer (mucosa) of the stomach wall. The tumor is often small (2 centimeters or less) and is not in any lymph nodes.

data.entity_name: Locoregional or locally advanced stomach cancer
data.content:
Locoregional or locally advanced stomach cancer
Locoregional or locally advanced stomach cancer has invaded other layers of the stomach wall and/or spread to the lymph nodes or organs near the stomach.

Metastatic stomach cancer
Metastatic stomach cancer has spread to other parts of the body, commonly affecting the liver, abdominal lining (peritoneum), distant lymph nodes, lungs, or bone.

Glioma
Glioma is a category of brain tumors that originate from glial cells, classified by histology, grade, and biomarkers.<SEP>Glioma is a type of brain tumor originating from glial cells, discussed as a separate medical condition in the text.<SEP>Glioma is a type of brain tumor that originates from glial cells, which support nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. It is characterized by the uncontrolled growth of glial cells and can disrupt normal brain function.<SEP>Glioma is a type of tumor characterized by the growth of abnormal cells in the brain or spinal cord, with varying grades (e.g., Grade 1, Grade 2, Grade 3, Grade 4) and distinct treatment approaches, including surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and targeted therapies.<SEP>Glioma is a type of tumor characterized by the growth of abnormal cells in the brain or spinal cord, with varying grades and treatment approaches.<SEP>Glioma is a type of tumor that grows in the brain, originating from glial cells and is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults.

Digestive system
The digestive system is a biological system responsible for taking in and breaking down food, absorbing nutrients, and removing waste from the body.

Adenocarcinomas
A type of cancer originating in glandular cells, typically found in colorectal cancers, contrasting with squamous cell carcinomas in anal cancer.<SEP>Adenocarcinomas are a type of stomach cancer that originates in cells lining the inside of the stomach wall and secrete mucus.

Testing for stomach cancer
Testing for stomach cancer involves a series of diagnostic procedures to determine the presence and stage of cancer, including blood tests, imaging, biopsies, and genetic risk assessments.

H. pylori tests
H. pylori tests detect the presence of Helicobacter pylori bacteria, a known risk factor for stomach cancer.

General health tests
General health tests evaluate overall health and medical history to identify risk factors or conditions that may contribute to cancer development.

Astrocytoma
Astrocytoma is a subtype of glioma that arises from astrocytes, a type of glial cell, and can vary in aggressiveness and prognosis.<SEP>Astrocytoma is a type of glioma that develops from astrocytes, which support nerve cell function in the central nervous system.<SEP>Astrocytoma is a type of glioma that resembles astrocytes, often classified by histology, grade, and biomarkers like IDH mutations.

Oligodendroglioma
Oligodendroglioma is a type of glioma that originates from oligodendrocytes, which protect electrical signaling in nerve cells.<SEP>Oligodendroglioma is a type of glioma that originates from oligodendrocytes, which support and insulate nerve cells in the central nervous system.

Glioblastoma
Glioblastoma is an aggressive and malignant subtype of glioma, often characterized by rapid growth and resistance to treatment.<SEP>Glioblastoma is the most destructive and dangerous type of glioma, arising from precursor cells that develop into astrocytes and oligodendrocytes.

Low-grade glioma
Low-grade glioma is a category of glioma characterized by slow growth and less aggressiveness, often associated with better prognosis compared to high-grade gliomas.<SEP>Low-grade glioma is a category of glioma that typically grows slowly and is less aggressive compared to high-grade gliomas.

High-grade glioma
High-grade gli, which is a category of glioma that tends to grow rapidly and is more aggressive, often leading to severe symptoms and complications.<SEP>High-grade glioma is a category of glioma characterized by rapid growth and increased aggressiveness, often leading to severe symptoms and complications.

Brain Tumor
A brain tumor is an abnormal growth of cells in the brain, encompassing various types including gliomas, and can cause neurological symptoms and complications.<SEP>A brain tumor is an abnormal growth of cells in the brain, which can cause various symptoms such as nausea, weakness, and changes in personality.

Low-Grade Glioma
Low-grade gliomas are slow-growing tumors that may not cause immediate symptoms and can develop for years before they’re diagnosed.<SEP>Low-grade gliomas are slow-growing tumors that may not cause immediate symptoms and can remain undetected for years.

High-Grade Glioma
High-grade gliomas are fast-growing, malignant tumors that often progress rapidly and require aggressive treatment approaches.

Headache
Headache is a common symptom of gliomas, often the first symptom in people with a glioma, and can be accompanied by nausea and vomiting.

Seizures
Seizures are frequent in people with brain tumors and are often an early sign of a glioma, especially in low-grade gliomas.

Fatigue
Fatigue is a common symptom of brain tumors, encompassing physical, cognitive, and emotional exhaustion.<SEP>Fatigue is a common symptom of gliomas, often debilitating and not related to sleep or activity levels.<SEP>Fatigue is a persistent tiredness or lack of energy often experienced by cancer survivors, which can impact daily activities and quality of life.

Nausea and Vomiting
Nausea and vomiting can be caused by the tumor putting increased pressure on the brain, often associated with glioma progression.

Lab Testing
Lab testing involves analyzing biological samples to identify glioma subtypes and guide treatment decisions.

Survival Statistics
Survival statistics provide data on patient outcomes for gliomas, though they may not reflect modern treatment advancements.

Gliomas
Gliomas are a type of brain tumor that can cause symptoms like vision problems, sensory disturbances, and blood clots.

Resection
Resection is a surgical procedure to remove as much of a tumor as possible, serving both as a diagnostic tool and a treatment method.<SEP>Resection is a surgical procedure to remove tissue, often used to excise bladder tumors for diagnosis or treatment.

Open Biopsy
Open biopsy is a surgical procedure to remove a tissue sample from a brain tumor, typically used when the tumor is in a difficult location.

Nausea
Nausea is a symptom caused by increased pressure from a brain tumor on the brain.

Vomiting
Vomiting is a symptom associated with brain tumors, often due to increased intracranial pressure.

Confusion
Confusion is a cognitive symptom of brain tumors, indicating impaired thinking or memory function.

Memory Loss
Memory loss is a symptom of brain tumors, reflecting damage to brain regions responsible for memory.

Speech Difficulties
Speech difficulties are symptoms of brain tumors affecting areas of the brain responsible for language and articulation.

Weakness
Weakness is a physical symptom of brain tumors, often presenting as muscle weakness on one side of the body.

Muscle Weakness
Muscle weakness is a specific manifestation of brain tumors affecting motor functions.

Balance
Balance issues are symptoms of brain tumors impacting coordination and spatial awareness.

Personality Changes
Personality changes are behavioral symptoms of brain tumors affecting mood-regulating brain regions.

Mood Changes
Mood changes are emotional symptoms of brain tumors, reflecting alterations in brain function.

Vision Problems
Vision problems are symptoms of brain tumors, including blurred vision, double vision, or loss of peripheral vision.

Blurred Vision
Blurred vision is a specific visual symptom of brain tumors affecting the visual pathways.

Double Vision
Double vision is a visual symptom caused by brain tumors disrupting eye coordination.

Loss of Peripheral Vision
Loss of peripheral vision is a visual symptom of brain tumors affecting the occipital lobe.

Sensory Disturbances
Sensory disturbances are symptoms of brain tumors, including numbness, tingling, or burning sensations.

Numbness
Numbness is a sensory symptom of brain tumors, often affecting one side of the body.

Tingling
Tingling is a sensory symptom of brain tumors, indicating nerve damage or irritation.

Burning Sensations
Burning sensations are sensory symptoms of brain tumors, often associated with nerve involvement.

Blood Clots
Blood clots are complications linked to high-grade gliomas, potentially causing leg swelling, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

Leg Swelling
Leg swelling is a symptom of blood clots associated with high-grade gliomas.

Chest Pain
Chest pain is a symptom of blood clots linked to high-grade gliomas.

Shortness of Breath
Shortness of breath is a symptom of blood clots associated with high-grade gliomas.

Cognitive Fatigue
Cognitive fatigue is a type of fatigue characterized by mental exhaustion and reduced cognitive function.

Emotional Fatigue
Emotional fatigue is a type of fatigue involving emotional exhaustion and mood changes.

Physical Fatigue
Physical fatigue is a type of fatigue marked by physical exhaustion and reduced energy levels.

External Sources
External sources are factors like noise that contribute to fatigue in patients with brain tumors.

Internal Sources
Internal sources are factors like medication or poor nutrition that contribute to fatigue in patients with brain tumors.

Medication
Medication is an internal source of fatigue that can affect patients with brain tumors.

Not Eating Properly
Not eating properly is an internal source of fatigue contributing to the symptoms of brain tumors.

Not Getting Enough Exercise
Not getting enough exercise is an internal source of fatigue affecting patients with brain tumors.

Provider
A provider is an organization or individual responsible for evaluating and managing the care of patients with brain tumors.

Parietal Lobe
The parietal lobe is a region of the brain responsible for processing sensory information and spatial awareness.

Occipital Lobe
The occipital lobe is a region of the brain responsible for processing visual information.

Neuropathologist
A neuropathologist is a medical professional specializing in the diagnosis of neurological conditions, including gliomas, by analyzing tissue samples and identifying biomarkers to classify tumors and guide treatment decisions.<SEP>A neuropathologist is a medical professional who tests tissue samples for specific biomarkers to aid in the diagnosis and classification of gliomas.<SEP>A neuropathologist is a specialist who examines tissue samples under a microscope to determine if a tumor is malignant or benign and to classify its type and grade.

Biomarkers
Biomarkers are molecular characteristics like genetic mutations (e.g., IDH gene) used to classify gliomas and predict their behavior.<SEP>Biomarkers are specific indicators found in the body that help in diagnosing and treating gliomas by providing information about the tumor's characteristics.<SEP>Biomarkers are specific indicators found in the body that help in diagnosing and treating gliomas by providing information about the tumor's genetic, molecular, and pathological characteristics, enabling personalized treatment strategies.

IDH gene
The IDH gene is a biomarker associated with certain gliomas, such as astrocytoma IDH-mutant, indicating genetic mutations that influence tumor growth and treatment.

Stereotactic biopsy
A stereotactic biopsy is a surgical procedure where a thin needle is used to remove a tumor sample under precise imaging guidance.

Open biopsy
An open biopsy involves a craniotomy to remove a tumor sample, requiring surgical tools and a larger incision compared to stereotactic methods.

Molecular testing
Molecular testing analyzes tumor samples for genetic markers and biomarkers to determine the tumor type, growth rate, and treatment options.

Pathology report
A pathology report is a document generated after analyzing biopsy samples, detailing tumor classification, malignancy, and molecular findings.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)
